reasons: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Nyctimene is the Lesbian girl turned into an owl, not Nycteus's daughter; Apollodorus gives Nycteus the daughter Antiope, and Hyginus has Nycteus father Nyctimene only in another tradition.
Apollodorus gives Circe as daughter of Helios and Perse (1.9.1), not Hecate. Only a late tradition makes Hecate her mother.
Hermes is father of Polybus of Sicyon's line (Pausanias) not Polybus of Corinth; in Apollodorus Polybus of Corinth, who raised Oedipus, has no such parentage.
Pausanias (Olympia) names Troilus, son of Alcinous, an Elean Olympic victor. This is a different Alcinous, not the Phaeacian king.
Alcetus son of Alcinous is an Elean boy-victor statue at Olympia, so another Alcinous than the Phaeacian king.
Corcyra was mother of Phaeax by Poseidon, and Phaeax's descendants include Nausithous. Alcinous is Nausithous's son, so Corcyra is at most a grandmother's line and not his mother.
Odyssey 7.56ff makes Alcinous the son of Nausithous, himself son of Poseidon and Periboea. Corcyra's son by Poseidon is Phaeax, so Alcinous is at most a descendant.
Arete was Alcinous's wife and niece, daughter of his brother Rhexenor, not his sister (Odyssey 7).

Hesiod's Sicyon is not Erechtheus's son. Pausanias (2.6.5) calls Sicyon son of Marathon or Metion, and Apollodorus has Metion as Erechtheus's brother-line, so Sicyon is another man's child at most a grandson-level confusion.
Pausanias' Henioche is daughter of Creon of Corinth (father of Glauce/Creusa), a different Creon, not the Theban.
Pausanias' Pyrrha belongs to the Corinthian Creon's family; confusion of two namesakes, not the Theban.
The Odyssey text says Arete is Rhexenor's daughter and Alcinous's niece and wife, so she is not his sibling. The link probably comes from a different tradition or a mix-up.
The Odyssey's own text says Arete was the daughter of Rhexenor, Alcinous' brother, so she is his niece and wife, not his sister. The Hesiod link is misread.

Apollodorus gives Aphidas (Apheidas of Tegea) as father of a different Stheneboea, wife of Proetus in a variant tradition, but Iobates is the usual father; Hesiod's Stheneboea is the Lycian king's daughter, and the book has no Aphidas.
The Doliones are a people, not a person; Apollonius makes Cyzicus their king, descended from Poseidon only loosely.
The Moliones (Eurytus and Cteatus) are twins; the Iliad names them sons of Molione, with Actor or Poseidon as father in some tradition. Treat as group of two; keep only as individuals.
Wikidata lists Tyro as spouse, but editor reads non-marriages as lovers; Tyro was seduced by Poseidon, so lover is right.
Hyrmina is a place in Elis, and Pausanias's Hyrmina is the daughter of Epeius, king of Elis, a different Epeius (son of Endymion) from the Trojan horse builder.
Anaxiroe was the wife of the Elean Epeius, son of Endymion, not the son of Panopeus.

Epicasta is not named as Nestor's daughter in the Odyssey; Homer gives Polycaste as the youngest daughter. The Hesiod link makes Epicasta a mother of Homer, which belongs to a different tradition and is not a Nestor-Epicasta link in this book.
Reversed: Pandora is Pyrrha's mother (Apollodorus, Theoi), so Pyrrha cannot be Pandora's parent.

Molus is the son of Deucalion of Crete (father of Idomeneus's line), not the son of Prometheus.
Apollodorus makes Actor a son of Phorbas or brother of Augeas only in a variant; Pausanias gives Augeas as son of Eleus, and Actor is a different figure, so the link is not supported in this book.

Agamede, wife of Mecistes in the Iliad, is a daughter of Augeas in the Iliad scholia, but Theoi's own listing does not cite her. The Iliad says only that she was Augeas' daughter, not mentioned in Pausanias; the link imports an unsupported tradition.
Hesione was given to Telamon as war prize after Heracles sacked Troy, mother of Teucer; a concubine, not a wife (Apollodorus). Editor's rule reads non-marriage spouse as lover.
Selene is the Moon goddess; the editor ruled Zeus as parent of Selene wrong, and Hesiod's Selene child Pandia is confused with Diana's cult.
Hesiod's Homeric Hymn tradition is mixed with Selene; editor has Selene-linked relations wrong, and Pandia belongs to Selene as child of Zeus only in a hymn, unsupported here.
Thalia the Grace and Thalia the Muse are confused; the editor rules Helios's Thalia wrong and this is a duplicate merge.

Eetion, Andromache's father, has no Zeus parentage in the Iliad.
Eetion of Thebe, Andromache's father, is not Zeus's son; the Hesiodic Eetion (Iasion, Demeter's lover, in Hesiod's Theogony) is a different man of the same name.
Xanthus the river or Trojan horse is not Zeus's son; the editor ties Xanthus to Midas.
Juno is both sister and wife of Jove; the book says she is his wife, so the sibling link should not be a spouse removal.
Wikidata and Hesiod give Metis as Zeus's first wife, but editor says only Hera/Juno is marriage, so this stays a lover.
Unsupported guess; no Iliad sentence names Truth as Zeus's child.
Macar is a Lesbian king in Pausanias, not Zeus's son.
Hermus is a river, unsupported as Zeus's son.
Eurus is born of Astraeus and Aurora in Hesiod's Theogony only for the three winds Zephyrus, Boreas, Notus; Eurus is not listed there and Wikidata's claim lacks ancient support.
Phaethon, son of Aurora and Cephalus, is a Pausanias-only tradition per the editor; in other books Phaethon is the son of Helios and Clymene, so this link does not belong here.
Pausanias does not make Hyperion a child of Agamemnon; Agamemnon's children are Orestes, Electra, Iphigenia, Chrysothemis, etc. The link likely confuses a different figure or misreads a sentence.

The quoted line is Aphrodite addressing Anchises as 'son of Dardanus', which is a generic descent phrase. Anchises' father is Capys, the son of Assaracus, and Dardanus is a remote ancestor, not his father.
The quoted line (Hymn to Aphrodite) calls Anchises 'son of Dardanus' only as a patronymic for the Dardanian line. Anchises' actual father is Capys, son of Assaracus, so Dardanus is a remote ancestor.
Pausanias reports the Cypriot claim that a Cypriot woman named Themisto was Homer's mother, which is a different Themisto from the Lapith princess, daughter of Hypseus and wife of Athamas.

Hesiod's Catalogue (and the Eugammon/Hellanicus tradition) has Telemachus marry Nestor's daughter Polycaste; she is a wife, not a lover. It is absent from the Odyssey itself, but the link comes from Hesiod.

The Catalogue of Women (Hesiod tradition) makes Polycaste Telemachus's wife, mother of Persepolis, so she was a wife and not just a lover; the editor's rule reads other spouse links as lovers, but this is an actual marriage.
Aethra slept with Aegeus once at Troezen and was never his wife, so by the editor's rule this is a lover link, not a marriage.
Apollodorus says Aegeus lay with Aethra at Troezen on a single night, which is a union and not a marriage; the editor's rule reads non-marriages as lovers.
Pausanias gives Oeneus a father Pandion (Athenian tradition) in a variant; Iliad and Theoi/Wikidata give Porthaon (Portheus) as father, so the Pandion link is another tradition not followed here.
Editor's rule: only marriages stay spouse links; Althaea is Oeneus' wife, Periboea is read as a secondary partner (Hesiod's tradition, Apollodorus), so mark as lover.
Duplicate spelling of Aegina, already linked as Asopus's daughter; this is the same person listed twice, so drop the duplicate node.
Cybele is not Saturn's wife in this book; his wife is Ops (Rhea), and Cybele is a separate Phrygian goddess merely conflated with Rhea.
Cybele is a Phrygian mother goddess, not Saturn's sister. Other books may mean Rhea under that name, but this is a confusion of two beings.
The Mecisteus line (son of Mecisteus, sprung of Talaus, who fought with Diomedes) is a different Eurypylus, the Argive. The Mysian Eurypylus is the son of Telephus and Astyoche.

The book's line (Catalogue of Ships-like passage) names Eurypylus as son of Mecisteus, so the link is stated by the book; but it is actually a mix-up: Euryalus is the son of Mecisteus, and the book's sentence gives Eurypylus.
Doris is Nereus' wife (daughter of Oceanus and Tethys per Hesiod); Apollodorus' link confuses her with a Nereid daughter.
Apollodorus 1.7.5 makes Endymion son of Aethlius and Calyce; Zeus as father is a variant from Wikidata that this book does not tell (Aethlius was son of Zeus).

Pausanias' Pierus is the Macedonian king who came to Thespiae and founded the Muses' cult there, and Wikidata gives Makedon as his father. Linus, the musician son of Amphiaraus or of Apollo, is another figure and is not Pierus' father.

In Ovid, Iole is Dryope's sister-in-law: Dryope says her father had Dryope's mother's child by another wife, and Iole is the daughter of Eurytus. Dryope is the daughter of Eurytus's wife's line, so the book calls them half-sisters at most, and the sentence names no sibling link to Iole directly. Actually Iole calls Dryope her sister, so the book supports a half-sibling link.
Arete is Alcinous's wife and niece, not his sibling. Odyssey 7 makes her daughter of Rhexenor, who was Alcinous's brother. Hesiod's sibling tie is a misreading.
Arete was Alcinous's niece and wife (daughter of his brother Rhexenor), not his sibling; the spouse link already covers the relationship.
Pyrrha is the wife of Deucalion, son of Prometheus, the flood hero Pindar tells of in Olympian 9. The Cretan Deucalion, son of Minos, is a different man, whose wife in Wikidata is Cleopatra.
Duplicate spelling of Deucalion; the same marriage is already kept under Deucalion, so this link is redundant. Merge with Deucalion.
No ancient source makes Juno the mother of Bellona. Her parentage is not given in Statius, and Wikidata's Juno link is an unsupported guess.
Bellona is a Roman war goddess with no ancient tradition naming Juno as her mother, so the link is unsupported.
No ancient source makes Jupiter the father of Bellona. Statius does not say so, and this link is an unsupported guess.
Bellona is a Roman war goddess, not Jove's child in the tradition.

link: Berenice lover_of Philip of Macedon, son of Amyntas
reasons: Pausanias' Berenice (wife of Ptolemy I, mother of Magas and Ptolemy II) is the Berenice who loved Philip, not Berenice Phernophorus; the Macedonian Philip of Pausanias' Magas passage is an obscure commoner, not Philip II's son Amyntas line, and Philip son of Amyntas is wrongly linked.
The Wikidata Berenice Phernophorus is Ptolemy II's daughter, but Pausanias' Berenice is the wife of Ptolemy I and mother of Magas, so this father link belongs to another Berenice.
Aethra lay with Aegeus at Troezen but was not his wife; the rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.
Æthra lay with Ægeus (and Poseidon) in one night at Troezen; she was not his wife, only a lover.
Pirithous was the son of Ixion (or Zeus) and Dia; Aethra is his namesake confusion, not his mother.
Æthra is the mother of Theseus, Pirithous' friend; Pirithous' mother is Dia (wife of Ixion), so the two are confused.
Pausanias' Phalanthus's wife is Aethra of Taras legend, a different Aethra from Pittheus' daughter; namesake.
Apollonius Rhodius (Argonautica 1.948) and Apollodorus make Cyzicus son of Aeneus and Aenete; Apollo as father is an unsupported Wikidata guess.
Erato in the Aeneid and Argonautica is a Muse, not Zeus's daughter by that name's namesake; the Aeneid's Erato is a Muse invoked, and the Argonautica's is likely a nymph — the match mixes beings.
Selene is a daughter of Hyperion and Theia; the editor rules Zeus is not her parent, and no lover tradition is given.
Pandora was made by Hephaestus and given by Zeus; she was not his lover.
Pallas is a Titan son of Crius, or the giant; not Zeus's child. Athena's epithet is a cult title.
Sisyphus is a son of Aeolus, not Zeus.
Sibyl is a title for several prophetesses; Pausanias gives Lamia or Theodorus as parent, not Zeus.
Macar is a son of Helios or Aeolus in tradition, not Zeus.
Xanthus is not a son of Zeus; the editor gives Midas as a parent in Hesiod.
Opportunity is an abstraction, not a person with Zeus as father.
Truth is a personification with no Zeus parentage fixed by the book.
Fortune is a personification; the parentage is an unsupported guess.
Hesiod makes Eris a daughter of Night.
Hermus is a river, with no known Zeus parentage.
Eetion is the father of Andromache or a son of Iasion; not Zeus's child.
The book's sentence names Ægialeus as son of Adrastus; Adrastus was Polynices' father-in-law, not his son. Polynices' son in the book is Thersander.
The Pausanias sentence lists Adrastus son of Talaus as an associate of Polynices on the expedition; it does not make Polynices his father. Talaus is his father.

Hippocoon's mother is Batea (daughter of Teleboas), wife of Oebalus, per Apollodorus; Gorgophone, Perseus' daughter, is Oebalus' other wife and mother of Tyndareus, so this link confuses the two wives.
Pausanias makes Hippocoon a rival of Tyndareus, a son of Oebalus by another mother (Batia in other sources); the book gives Gorgophone only Tyndareus.
Hesiod's tradition has Hermes lie with Dryops' daughter, mother of Pan; this was a union, not a marriage, and only marriages count as spouse.
Mars is the son of Jupiter and Juno; Mercury is the son of Jupiter and Maia, so they are only half-brothers, and Statius does not make them siblings by mother.
Mercury is son of Jupiter and Maia, so only a half-brother; Statius does not make them full siblings, and the link is unsupported.
Pindar's odes name no such child; Fame is a personification and no genealogy supports this link.

Editor decided Jove is not Pasithea's parent. Pasithea is a Grace in Iliad 14 and Pausanias, not Hera's child, and Theoi lists Hera as her mother only loosely, so the link is unsupported in this book.
The Graces are children of Zeus and Eurynome; the editor already rules Helios the father of Aglaea and Thalia wrong, so the group link goes too.
Pindar says Helios 'lay with' Rhodos; only marriages count as spouse links, so this is read as a lover link.
Amalthea is the nurse of Zeus; a Helios parentage is a doubtful variant. It is unsupported in this book.

link: Amphion, son of Antiope spouse_of Niobe
reasons: Amphion's wife is Niobe daughter of Tantalus; Pausanias mentions both Niobes, and the Argive Niobe (daughter of Phoroneus) is a different being, so this spouse belongs to the Theban Niobe.
Chloris is the daughter of Amphion's Niobe (daughter of Tantalus), not the Argive Niobe.
Tantalus is father of the Theban Niobe turned to stone, not the Argive Niobe daughter of Phoroneus.

Hesperus (the evening star) is son of Astraeus and Eos in Hesiod's Theogony only as Eosphorus; Hesperus as her son is a confusion, though Ovid/Apollonius treat Hesperus as son of Cephalus or Atlas, so unsupported here.

Pausanias gives Phaethon as son of Cephalus; Hesiod's Phaethon is son of Eos and Cephalus, so the editor's decision on Cephalus is the right link, but Aurora as parent is a variant of the same story and should be kept.

link: Helice parent_of Ion, son of Xuthus
reasons: Pausanias says Bura was Ion's daughter by Helice, so Helice is Ion's wife, not his parent; the link reverses the relation. The spouse link already covers her.
Demodoce is the daughter of the Argive/Arcadian Agenor's line in other tradition; Hesiod's Agenor is not clearly the Phoenician king.
Pausanias' Crotopus is the Argive son of Agenor, son of Triopas or Phorbas, a different Agenor.
Iphidamas is the Trojan son of Antenor, a confusion with a different Agenor/Antenor.
Preugenes is the Achaean son of Agenor of Patrae, a different Agenor.
Echeclus is the Trojan son of Agenor (Iliad), a different Agenor.
Pausanias names Piras as a father of Styx's namesake or a river figure; Hesiod has no such husband, and the link confuses two beings. The flag is justified for Piras only.
Anchises' father is Capys, son of Assaracus, son of Tros; Dardanus is a distant ancestor (Iliad 20.215-240), so he is not the parent.
Anchises was son of Capys and grandson of Assaracus, not of Dardanus; the line runs Dardanus, Erichthonius, Tros, Assaracus, Capys, Anchises. Hesiod does not make Dardanus his father.

Odyssey 12 names Neaera as mother of Helios' daughters Phaethusa and Lampetia; Apollonius' Argonautica names no mother, and Clymene (Klymene) is a different mother, mainly of Phaethon and the Heliades, so this link confuses two beings.
Pausanias names Hyperion as a son of Aegisthus-era Orestes' line, not of Agamemnon; Hyperion is a Titan or a different figure, so this is a misreading or confusion with another being.
Anaxibia is Agamemnon's sister (daughter of Atreus) in some sources, or the wife of Nestor; Pausanias does not make her his daughter, so it is a confusion with another Anaxibia.
Pasithea is a Grace, daughter of Zeus and Eurynome (or Hera); Dionysus is not her father in the Iliad or the tradition it follows. The editor rules Jove and Bromius as her parent wrong everywhere.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses the daughter of Dryops is Dryope, whose sister is Iole, wife of Andraemon, not Eurytus' daughter Iole; Apollodorus makes Iole the daughter of Eurytus.
Hesiod (Theogony) and Wikidata make Themis Zeus's second wife, not merely a lover; the site's rule reads non-Hera spouses as lovers, but Themis is traditionally a wife.
A group label, not a person. Apollodorus names the sons Mermerus and Pheres, and the individual links cover them.
Eriopis is Jason's wife or sister in other traditions, not clearly his daughter in Apollodorus; Pausanias does not make her a child of Jason and Medea.
Harmonia is Mars's daughter and married Cadmus. Mars was not her husband.
In Statius, Venus is Mars's lover. In the Iliad Aphrodite is the daughter of Zeus and Dione, so she is no sibling of Ares by the same parents. The lover link already exists.
Mars is Venus's lover in the Thebaid, not her brother. In the Iliad, Ares and Aphrodite are children of Zeus but not full siblings. Statius has Venus in Mars's embrace.
Duplicate spelling of Penthesilea, which is already listed as Mars's child. Merge the two.

Mercury is the son of Jupiter and Maia. He is called 'brother' in Statius only as a half-brother, but Mars's mother is Juno, so the tie is a loose half-sibling. Keep the sentence as the book's own phrasing.

In the Thebaid Mars addresses Mercury as 'brother' only in a loose sense; Mercury is son of Jove and Maia, Mars son of Jove and Juno, so a full sibling link is not supported, and the line is just a courteous address.
Apollo's twin is Artemis; the Moon (Selene) is a different being, a Diana/Selene conflation in Metamorphoses. The editor has also ruled that Selene is not Apollo's relative.
Several figures are named Kyknos; the Wikidata link is unsupported in this book and likely belongs to a different Kyknos (Ares's son in Pindar).
Scylla is the daughter of Phorcys or Crataeis (Phorbas or Hecate in other versions); Apollo as father is a mix-up with another Scylla, Nisus's daughter, or a misreading in Hesiod's fragments.
Pindar describes a bridal bed and 'common wedlock' for Apollo and Kyrene, so it is a marriage.
Same figure as Kyrene; Pindar describes wedlock, and the duplicate spelling should be merged.
Alcinous is son of Nausithous (Odyssey); in Apollonius Corcyra is the island nymph loved by Poseidon, whose son was Phaeax by tradition, not Alcinous.
Corcyra (Asopus' daughter) was mother of Phaeax by Poseidon in some accounts and is linked to Nausithous's line only through confusion; no source in Argonautica gives her as Alcinous' mother.
Hermes's son Polybus is a different man (Pausanias' Polybus of Sicyon context); the Odyssey's Polybus is father of Eurymachus (Ithacan), with no Hermes parentage in the book.

Electra here is the Pleiad who bore Harmonia to Zeus, or the Samothracian Electra, and she is not a daughter of Agenor. Pausanias links her to Cadmus only through Samothrace, which confuses the two Electras.

Metamorphoses uses Hermione as another name for Harmonia, Cadmus's wife; the tree has made a separate person out of it. Hermione, daughter of Menelaus, is a different figure, so the link duplicates Harmonia.
Cadmus' wife was Harmonia (Hermione is a variant spelling in Metamorphoses), not Menelaus' daughter.
Rhadamanthys married Alcmena only in a late tradition (after Heracles' death, per Apollodorus/Pherecydes); Hesiod doesn't say it, and the editor's rule reads non-primary spouses as lovers.

Per Apollodorus and Pausanias, Rhadamanthys married Alcmena after Amphitryon's death in Boeotia; the editor's rule treats any non-marriage as a lover, but this was a marriage, so it stays a spouse link.

Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, is said in the Thesprotian tradition (Eugammon's Telegony) to have married Odysseus after his wanderings, which makes her a marriage in that tradition. But the editor's rule is that only the Penelope marriage counts, so any other spouse link is read as a lover.
Mausolus' wife was Artemisia II of Caria, his sister; Artemisia I (Xerxes' ally at Salamis, Herodotus 7.99) was daughter of Lygdamis, a generation earlier, so the link belongs to the namesake.
Pausanias' Spartan hero-chapel concerns a different Ægeus, son of Œolycus (a Theban/Spartan Aegeid line), not the Athenian king, son of Pandion.
The Daughters of Pelias (the Peliades) are a group, not one person. They should be individual links to Alcestis, Asteropea, Antinoe and others, not a single group node.
Pausanias's Acusilaus is the Rhodian boxer, son of Diagoras of Rhodes, not the Argive logographer, son of Cabas or Scabras.

This is a different Stheneboea, the Arcadian daughter of Aphidas and sister of Aleus, who also married Proetus in the book's Arcadian genealogy. The Lycian queen Stheneboea (Antia) is the daughter of Iobates or Amphianax, so the two are conflated under one name.
Cadmus's sister Electra is a different Electra (Pausanias), a daughter of Atlas or Agenor's line; Aeschylus' Electra is Agamemnon's daughter and has no brother Cadmus.
Hercyna is a nymph of Lebadea; Pausanias (9.39.2-4) calls her a girl who played with Core, not a daughter of Trophonius, so the link is unsupported.
Anubis is an Egyptian god (child of Osiris/Nephthys or Set); no Greek source makes Typhon his father, only a late Wikidata association with Set-Typhon.
Typhoeus is the Greek monster; Wikidata's Egyptian father is Seth (whom Greeks equated with Typhon), but Metamorphoses never makes Typhoeus Anubis's father, so this is a misidentified namesake link.

Hesiod Theogony 304-325 has Echidna bear Typhon's children as his mate, and Wikidata lists her as his spouse; the editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers, but this is a standard pairing, so keep as spouse.
Typhon is Echidna's mate (Hesiod, Wikidata lists him as spouse), so treat as spouse.

Sciron is the son-in-law of Pylas in tradition (Pylas gave his daughter to Pandion; Sciron is separate). Plutarch and Pausanias make Sciron a Megarian, but Pylas as father of Sciron is not supported; Pausanias does not state this.
Cercopes line names Theia and Ocean as parents, but Ocean's wife is Tethys; per editor's rule, other spouse links read as lovers.
The book's Cercopes sentence says only that Theia and Ocean had sons, not that they married; Hesiod gives Hyperion as her husband, so under the editor's rule Ocean is read as a lover.
A chorus is a group, not a person; the individual Oceanids are already listed.
Hesiod's Gaia/Uranus descent is not Ovid's. Metamorphoses 4.453 makes the Furies daughters of Night (Nyx), so this link follows a different tradition from the book.

Hesiod's Uranus descent is not Ovid's. Metamorphoses 4.453 calls the Furies daughters of Night (Nyx), so this link follows a different tradition from the book.
In the Aeneid (2.340) Dymas is a Trojan warrior who fights beside Aeneas and is killed in the night battle; he is not the Phrygian king Dymas, Hecuba's father in some traditions.
Pausanias's Aethra wife of Phalanthus is a Spartan/Tarentine Aethra, daughter of Oebalus? a different woman from Pittheus's daughter, the mother of Theseus.
Apollodorus (3.12.3) makes Tithonus a son of Laomedon; the Cephalus link confuses him with Cephalus's son Phaethon, whom Eos also carried off, and rests on a Wikidata conflation.
Dexamenus of Olenus is father of a different Eurypylus (Heracles' kin, Pausanias 7.19); the Iliad's Thessalian Eurypylus is son of Euaemon (Iliad 2.736), so the two Eurypyluses are confused.
In Aeneid, Latinus is son of Faunus (and Marica), and Faunus is the Roman counterpart, not Pan himself; the link confuses Pan with Faunus.
Pindar's 'Hermes' daughter Fame' (Olympian 8) is a poetic personification of Angelia, the messenger. It is a figure of speech and not a mythic child.
Hesiod has Hermes lie with Dryops' daughter, mother of Pan, with no marriage. Under the editor's rule, any non-listed spouse link is a lover.

In Ovid's Metamorphoses 14, Hersilia is the wife of Romulus (Quirinus), and the book never calls her Tatius's daughter; the tradition making her his daughter is a rare one. Plutarch and Livy more often tie her to the Sabine women or to Hostus Hostilius, so the link is not supported by this book.

Telegonus marrying Penelope is a late sequel tradition (Telegony; Hesiod's Catalogue has Circe's sons), not Pausanias' account, but it is a real marriage after Odysseus' death, not a lover link; keep as a marriage only from hesiod, not here.</br>
Apollodorus (1.9.13) makes Bias the husband of Pero, and Talaus is the son of Bias and Pero in tradition; but the link is listed as parent_of Talaus, which is actually correct, so this is not wrong.
Morn is Pindar's word for Dawn (Eos), a common noun for the goddess, not a separate person; the passage means Eos, so this is a duplicate of Eos as mother, not a distinct parent.

Callisto is the Arcadian nymph who became the Bear and mother of Arcas; she is not Faunus's mother. Wikidata and tradition (Virgil) give Faunus as son of Picus and Canens, and the Metamorphoses never makes Callisto his mother.
Ovid gives Calisto only Arcas; Faunus is a Roman Pan-figure with no tie to Calisto, an unsupported guess from the Pan confusion.
Nessus the centaur is the son of Ixion and the cloud Nephele, the Ixion figure, not the Nephele who bore Phrixus and Helle (Athamas's wife).
Oceanus as father is attached to the Athamas Nephele by Wikidata, but Theoi lists no such parentage and the Ixion cloud was shaped by Zeus; the link is unsupported and mixes the two figures.
Metanira's son Demophon is the Eleusinian child nursed by Demeter; Hesiod's Demophon is the son of Theseus, so the link belongs to a namesake.
Pausanias' Polydorus son of Alcamenes is the Spartan king, not the Theban son of Cadmus.
Polydorus is the son of the Spartan king Alcamenes, not of the sculptor.
Eurycrates son of Polydorus belongs to the Spartan king Polydorus, not the Theban.
Hesiod's Demodoce, daughter of an Agenor, belongs to a different Agenor (a Calydonian or Argive figure), not the son of Poseidon and Libya.
Pausanias's Crotopus is the son of Agenor of Argos, a descendant of Phoroneus, not the Phoenician king.
Iphidamas is the son of the Trojan Antenor, a different figure whose name is close to Agenor.
Preugenes belongs to the Argive Agenor, father of Crotopus in Pausanias's Achaean line.
Echeclus, son of Agenor, is the Trojan Echeclus killed by Achilles, from a different Agenor.
Calus (Talos/Perdix) is Daedalus's nephew, the son of his sister, not his sibling; the link is unsupported by Pausanias.
Hesiod's Menoetius is the Titan, son of Iapetus and brother of Atlas, not Patroclus' father, who is Menoetius son of Actor. It also duplicates the correct Menoetius link.
Pausanias (6.9) makes Pantias of Chios the pupil of his father Sostratus, a sculptor of Chios, not Sostratus of Dyme, the beloved of Heracles; the sentence does not concern the Dyme figure.

Pausanias makes Triptolemus a daughter-of-Cercyon's kin (Cercyon's daughter Alope's line) only in his own telling; Apollodorus never links them, and Cercyon the Eleusinian wrestler is not Apollodorus's sibling for Triptolemus, so the link is imported from another book.
Editor's rule: only marriages count as spouse links. Glauce (Creusa) is Jason's later bride in Apollodorus, not a wife in this book, so she is read as a lover.
This is a group, not a person. The sons are already listed by name (Mermerus, Pheres, etc.), so the group node duplicates them.
Anubis is the child of Osiris/Nephthys in Egyptian myth; this comes from the Isis match, not from Ovid's Io, whose only child is Epaphus.
Io (as Isis) is not Anubis's mother in Ovid; Egyptian tradition gives Nephthys, and Io is only identified with Isis, so this confuses two beings.
In the Odyssey (3.282) Phrontis is Menelaus' helmsman, son of Onetor, not the Argonautic son of Phrixus and Chalciope.
Hesiod has no Aidos child of Prometheus; unsupported, likely a misread of Hesiod's Aidos.
Pausanias' Aetnaeus is not a son of Prometheus in the tradition; unsupported.
This is a group label (the children Medea killed), not a person. The sons are already named individually as Mermerus and Pheres.
Hesiod (Theogony 306-325) and Apollodorus make Echidna Typhon's mate and the mother of his monstrous brood; Wikidata also lists her as his spouse, so she was a mate rather than a mere lover.
Endeis, Peleus' mother (daughter of Chiron or Sciron), is not Thetis' sister. Thetis' sisters are the Nereids, daughters of Nereus and Doris.
Phocus son of Aeacus was Peleus' half-brother, whom Peleus killed. His mother was Psamathe, a different Nereid. He is not Thetis' son.
Pausanias does not name Evander as her son. Echemus and Timandra's son is Laodocus in the tradition; the Arcadian Evander is son of Hermes and a nymph (Carmenta/Themis), so this is a confusion.
Pausanias says Evander's mother was a Nymph, daughter of Ladon. Timandra is the mother of the Evander of Pallene in a different tradition, so the link comes from a namesake.
Tecmessa was a captive taken as concubine by Aias (Sophocles' Ajax), not a wife; the editor's rule treats non-marriage links as lover.
Deidameia bore Neoptolemus to Achilles on Scyros but was not a marriage; the editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.
Helen's union with Achilles is a post-death tradition on Leuke (Pausanias) and not a marriage; the editor reads it as a lover link.
Achilles and Helen on the White Island is a late tale, not a marriage; treat as a lover.

link: Achilles parent_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
reasons: Pyrrhus of Epirus is a historical king who claimed descent from Achilles; the mythic Pyrrhus is another name for Neoptolemus, already linked as his son.
Hyrieus is son of Poseidon and Alcyone (Pleiad) in the usual tradition; Learchus (son of Athamas) is a confusion, not his father.
Learchus died as a child, killed by Athamas (Pausanias 1.44.7); Hyrieus is the son of Poseidon and Alcyone or Clonie, or of Thebes tradition, not of Learchus.

link: Hercules parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
reasons: A group of children, not a person; the individual sons are the proper links.
Gaia is not Poseidon's lover in any cited source; unsupported guess.
Editor: Aegeus and Aethra are Theseus's parents only in Pausanias; for Pindar the tree keeps Poseidon only in tradition, but not confirmed here.

Editor ruled wrong everywhere.
Sarpedon the Lycian is son of Zeus; Poseidon's son Sarpedon of Thrace is a different person (namesake).
The Doliones are a people, not a person; group taken for a person.
Moliones are the twin sons of Molione; the Iliad is cited, the twins' father is Actor or Poseidon, a variant.
Cteatus is son of Actor/Molione, with Poseidon only a variant paternity.
Wikidata lists Tyro as a spouse, though the myth makes her a lover.
Pausanias' Thalpius son of Eurytus belongs to Eurytus son of Actor (a Molionid, Eurytus of Elis), not Eurytus of Oechalia.
Pausanias' Theraphone, wife of Eurytus, belongs to the Molionid Eurytus, not the king of Oechalia.
Ixion's father is Phlegyas (or Antion/Leonteus/Aeton in other versions); Ares as father is an unsupported guess, and Metamorphoses gives no father for him.
Ixion is the son of Phlegyas (or Antion), not Mars; Wikidata confuses the line.

Nessus is a centaur, one of the offspring of Ixion and the cloud in some versions, but Metamorphoses names no parent for him, and the tradition usually treats him as a son of Centaurus or Ixion only loosely; the link is unsupported here.

link: Urania parent_of Linus, son of Urania
reasons: Two different Linuses are joined under one name: Hesiod's Linus son of Urania and Pausanias' Linus son of Apollo are distinct traditions; the Linus son of Apollo link should be tied to a different mother (Psamathe or Calliope in other tellings), not Urania.

link: Urania parent_of Linus, son of Apollo
reasons: Pausanias gives Linus as son of Apollo by Psamathe (Argive Linus) and Urania appears as his mother only in the separate Hesiodic Linus; the two Linuses are confused.
Hesiod (Theogony) makes Themis Zeus's second wife, and Wikidata lists Zeus as her spouse. The editor's rule only turns spouse links into lovers for Zeus and Hera or Juno, so Themis stays a wife.
Anchises' father is Capys, son of Assaracus, son of Tros; Dardanus is a more distant ancestor (great-great-grandfather), not his parent.

Pausanias' Diophanes, son of Diaeus, is the Achaean League's Diophanes of Megalopolis (earlier, 3rd–2nd c. BC, father of a different man), while Diaeus of Megalopolis was the last strategos in 150–146 BC. The Diaeus who fathered Diophanes is a different, earlier man of the same name.

Anius's daughters are a group, not a single person. Metamorphoses 13 has Anius say he fathered five children (a son and four daughters, the Oenotropae), so the link is plausible but cannot be a person node.

Parthenopaeus was son of Atalanta with Melanion or Meleager (Apollodorus 3.9.2), or Ares; the cited Pausanias sentence about Asphodicus's tomb says nothing of Talaus. Talaus' sons were Adrastus, Parthenopaeus is sometimes given as Talaus' son in Aeschylus/Euripides? No, mainstream is Atalanta's son.
The cited sentence is about Asphodicus' tomb and says nothing of Talaus; Talaus was father of Adrastus, and Parthenopaeus is son of Atalanta by Melanion (or Meleager/Ares).

Aristomachus son of Talaus is a rare variant not stated in Hesiod's text; Aristomachus is usually son of Talaus only in Apollodorus 1.9.13 as a brother of Adrastus, so keep is arguable, but the book gives no support.
Ares as father of Ixion is a doubtful Wikidata entry among five candidates; Pindar (Pythian 2) gives no father, and the usual tradition names Phlegyas (or Antion/Peirithous's line), not Ares.
Ixion is son of Phlegyas (or Antion), not of Ares; Ares is only Phlegyas' father.

In Argonautica, Idmon is the son of Apollo and Asteria (or Cyrene per some Wikidata claims) — the book names Aristaeus as Cyrene's son, and Apollonius gives Idmon's mother as Cyrene only in some scholia; nothing in this book supports it.

Idmon's mother in Apollonius is not Cyrene; Cyrene is Aristaeus' mother by Apollo, and she is not named as Idmon's mother in this book. Other traditions name Asteria or Antianeira (Theoi/Wikidata), so this looks like a confusion with Aristaeus.

Metra is the daughter of Erysichthon, wife of Autolycus's namesake? In Ovid's Metamorphoses (8.738ff) she is Erysichthon's daughter, who shapeshifts and is sold; Hyginus later gives her as Autolycus's... no ancient marriage is in Pausanias, and the book names only Neaera as wife; the link is unsupported here.
Aratus the poet of Sicyon was son of Clinias and Aristodama (editor: right only in Pausanias), not a child of Asclepius; this is a namesake confusion.
Direction reversed: Apollodorus (and Hesiod's tradition) makes Pandora Pyrrha's mother, not her daughter; Pandora is the first woman and Pyrrha is her daughter.
Apollodorus calls Amphictyon an autochthonous king of Attica, not a son of Deucalion and Pyrrha; only Hellen, Protogeneia and others are their children.

The Phaethon son of Eos is the one by Cephalus, a tradition the editor limits to Pausanias. In Hesiod, Phaethon is Eos's son by Tithonus, but Apollodorus and others use the name for Helios's son. It does not suit the Fall of Troy, where Eos's son is Memnon.
Harmonia was wife of Cadmus; the editor's rule reads any non-marriage 'spouse' link as a lover. Ares was her father or lover per tradition, not husband; Argonautica names her as his child/lover.
Panic (Phobos/Deimos-like personification) is not a person; Theoi lists Phobos and Deimos as sons, but 'Panic' as a child is a loose personification, not a being; keep only if tied to Phobos.
Hermes is son of Zeus and Maia, so a half-brother at most; Statius' mention is not a sibling statement from Hera.
Euryphaessa is Hyperion's wife in the Homeric Hymn. Hesiod does not make her his sister. The sibling link confuses the two names (Theia and Euryphaessa).
Midas is a mortal Phrygian king, not a child of Rhea; in Ovid's Metamorphoses Rhea/Cybele is only his patron deity, so the link confuses Midas with her divine children.

link: Sisyphus parent_of Glaucus, son of Sisyphus
reasons: This is a duplicate node for Glaucus, son of Sisyphus. In Apollodorus 2.3.1 he is the same Glaucus already linked as Sisyphus's son, so the duplicate should be removed.
Polypemon is the father of Procrustes (Damastes), not Sinis; the link confuses the two bandits. Sinis's father is Poseidon or Polypemon's son Procrustes per Wikidata/Plutarch variants, not Polypemon.

Pityocamptes (Sinis) is a different bandit, usually son of Polypemon by Sylea in some accounts, but in Pausanias Sinis is a separate figure; Wikidata mixes Procrustes with Polypemon, father of Sinis. Procrustes/Damastes is a different bandit from Sinis's father.
Pausanias quotes Chœrilus saying Cercyon's mother was a daughter of Amphictyon (Alope), and Cercyon's father was Poseidon; Amphictyon is Cercyon's grandfather, not parent.
In Hesiod's Theogony Earth (Gaia) is born from Chaos, before Night and Day; Day cannot be her parent, and Theoi's listing does not support it.
Phaethon's mother is the Oceanid Clymene wife of Merops in Ovid/Argonautica tradition, not Hesiod's Clymene wife of Iapetus; in Hesiod's book this is a different being.
The Heliades are daughters of Clymene wife of Merops (Ovid), a different Clymene from Iapetus' wife.
Apollodorus' Clymene, daughter of Minyas, is mother of Atalanta by Iasus; unrelated to the Oceanid.
This is Clymene daughter of Minyas (Scholiast on Od. xi.326), not the Oceanid; belongs with Iphiclus and Atalanta.

link: Clymene parent_of Iphiclus, son of Phylacus
reasons: Iphiclus' mother is Clymene daughter of Minyas, not the Oceanid wife of Iapetus.
Pindar's Deinis and his father Meges are Aeginetan race winners (Nemean 7), not the Epeian Meges son of Phyleus at Troy.
Metamorphoses names only Venus as Cupid's parent ("son of Venus", "Cupid, my son"); Mars as father comes only from Wikidata's variant tradition, which Ovid does not tell.
Cupid is son of Venus; Ovid does not make Mars his father, and the usual tradition (Hesiod, Homeric hymns) disagrees, though some late sources say Ares. Wikidata's claim is a minor variant.
The Doliones are a people, not a person. Their eponym Dolion is the son of Poseidon in the tradition.
Podaleirius is the son of Asclepius in the Iliad, not of Poseidon.
Rhea is the mother of Zeus, Hera and their siblings, not of Enyalios; Wikidata gives Enyo as mother, and Pindar names no parent for him.
Enyalios is usually an epithet of Ares, son of Zeus and Hera; no ancient source makes Rhea his mother.
Enyalios is early on identified with Ares as an epithet or aspect (Iliad), so listing Ares as his father makes the god his own father; Wikidata's father link is a confusion of identity.
Enyalios is a cult title or epithet of Ares, not a separate son.

Aeneas's wife Creusa was a Trojan, daughter of Priam; Pausanias' Creusa is the Athenian daughter of Erechtheus, whose husband was Xuthus. The Pausanias passage names Clymene, Aristomache and others, not Aeneas as her husband. The Aeneas link belongs to the Trojan Creusa.

Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, bore Polypoetes to Ulysses after his return (Eugammon's Telegony tradition); this was not a lasting marriage, and the editor reads any spouse other than Penelope as a lover.
In Pausanias the river Alpheus loves Artemis but is refused and she escapes; a pursuer, not her lover, and the Argonautica tells no such story.

Pausanias' Pythagoras, father of the Elean wrestler Caprus, is a different man, a Samian athlete's namesake. Pausanias also treats Pythagoras the Wise separately, as son of Mnesarchus. The philosopher is not Caprus' father.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses the Pierides are daughters of a Macedonian Pierus and Evippe, who is a different man from Hesiod's Pierus, father of Oeager, so the link belongs to the other Pierus.
Evippe is the wife of the Pierus of Metamorphoses; in this book Pierus's partner is the nymph Methone.
Oenone was a nymph he lived with before Helen (Apollodorus), not a formal marriage; editor's rule reads non-marriages as lovers. Hesiod does not mention her.
Alcetus and Troilus are not children of the Phaeacian Alcinous in Odyssey or Apollodorus; the Pausanias attribution likely confuses another person of that name.
Troilus is a son of Priam or Apollo; the link confuses another figure with Alcinous.
Aeneas' wife Creusa, daughter of Priam, is a different person from the Athenian Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus, who married Xuthus.
Apollonius Rhodius (Argonautica 1.948) makes Cyzicus son of Aeneus and Aenete; Apollo as father is an unsupported Wikidata addition.
In the Argonautica Cyzicus is son of Aeneus and Aenete, king of the Doliones, not Apollo's son.
Doris is Nereus' wife and the mother of the Nereids (Hesiod, Theogony), not his daughter; Doris spouse_of Nereus is the correct link.
Hesiod's Selene is the moon goddess, daughter of Hyperion; the editor ruled Zeus is not her parent, and she is not his lover.
Pandia is the daughter of Zeus and Selene only in the Homeric Hymn; the editor rejected the Selene link, so this one is unsupported.
Pallas, the Titan or giant, is confused with Athena Pallas; Athena is already listed as Minerva.
Pandora was made by Hephaestus at Zeus's order; she was not his lover.
Hermus is a river; Hesiod does not make Zeus his father.
Hesiod's Eetion is Iasion, who is already listed separately.
The Graces are a group; the individual Graces are already listed.
The Muses are a group; the individual Muses are already listed.
A group, not a person.
A group, not a person.
Opportunity (Kairos) is an abstraction; Pausanias only mentions an altar, and no father is stated.
Truth is an abstraction; Zeus is not stated as her father in this book.
Macar is not a son of Zeus in the sources; Macareus is a descendant of Aeolus, not of Zeus.
The editor says that Lamia and Theodorus are the Sibyl's parents in Pausanias, so Zeus is not her parent.
The editor rules this link wrong everywhere.
This is the Milesian boy boxer Antipater, son of Clinopater, not the Macedonian regent.
This is Antipater son of Cassander and Thessalonice, who killed his mother, a grandson of the regent.

link: Antipater sibling_of Philip, son of Cassander
reasons: The sentence is about Cassander's sons, so the Antipater here is Cassander's son, not the regent.
Hesiod (Theogony) and Wikidata treat Echidna as Typhon's mate, and Apollodorus has Typhon beget Orthus, the Chimera and the Sphinx on her; this is a marriage, not a mere affair.
Typhon is Echidna's mate in Hesiod and Apollodorus, and Wikidata lists him as spouse.
Rhadamanthus is a son of Zeus and Europa (Apollodorus); Hephaestus is not his father in any source.
Mulciber is Vulcan/Hephaestus; Rhadamanthus is son of Zeus and Europa (Apollodorus, Homer's Iliad). Wikidata's Hephaestus father is a confusion.
Idomeneus was the son of Deucalion and so grandson of Minos (Iliad, Odyssey); Pausanias is loose here.
Pausanias' Lycus son of Pandion is the Athenian hero of the Lyceum and the Great Goddesses, not the Theban regent.
Thrasybulus, son of Lycus, is the Athenian general, whose father was an Athenian Lycus, not the Theban king.
The sentence only mentions Phidolas' sons winning a horse race; it says nothing of a son Lycus.
Pausanias' Asterion is a different Cretan figure (Asterion/Asterius, Minos' stepfather in tradition); Minos' son is not that Asterion in this book's tradition.
Themistinoe is not known as a daughter of Ceyx of Trachis; the link appears to come from Hesiod's tree and is unsupported for Pausanias.
In the Iliad Ares is son of Zeus and Hera, and Aphrodite is daughter of Zeus and Dione; they are half-siblings at most, and the Odyssey makes them lovers.
Venus is Mars' lover in the Odyssey (Demodocus' song); Aphrodite is not his sister in Homer's tradition, and the Iliad has her as Zeus' daughter, not Hera's.
Panic (Phobos/Deimos group) is the child of Ares and Aphrodite only as personified Fear; 'Panic' as a person is a group or misreading, not a distinct child.
Pausanias (2.18.6; 3.18.13) calls Nicostratus a son of Menelaus by a slave woman, Pieris the Aetolian, not by Helen; Hesiod's Helen has only Hermione. Helen is not his mother in this book.
Nicostratus is a son of Menelaus (by a slave woman in Odyssey/Pausanias tradition), not Helen's; Odyssey and Pausanias give Helen only Hermione.
Pan as son of Callisto is not in Pausanias; the editor ruled Dryops' daughter as Pan's mother right only in Hesiod, and this link comes only from Wikidata.
Anaxiroe is a daughter of Coronus and wife of Epeus in no standard source; Pausanias links Anaxiroe to Epeius only dubiously, and the Aeneid never mentions a wife, so the link is unsupported.
Hyrmina is a place/eponym tied to Elean Epeius (king of Elis, Endymion's son), a namesake of the Trojan horse builder, not Panopeus' son.
Editor ruled this wrong everywhere; Aeschylus (Suppliants 305, Prometheus Bound 566) makes Argus a son of Earth (Gaia).
Editor's decision: Inachus as parent of Argus is wrong everywhere; Argus Panoptes is son of Aristor (or Arestor) and Argus of Argos descends from Zeus and Niobe.
Pausanias (1.2.5 area) gives Cleogenes as a son of a different Silenus figure; in Apollodorus this link has no support and Theoi lists no such child for the Dionysian Silenus.

The quoted sentence only says Hercules sided with Lycus in a battle against the king of the Bebryces; it names no Mygdon and no sibling. Mygdon appears there as a fellow king of Mysia/Phrygia and is not called Amycus' brother.
In Fall of Troy (Quintus), 'Pallas' is the goddess Athena, whom Zeus bore from his head; the Wikidata Pallas is Athena's friend, daughter of Triton, so the Zeus link comes from mixing the two.
Clytus son of Pallas in Metamorphoses is a different Pallas (the Titan or Evander's line), not the goddess Athena, who is a virgin.
Butes son of Pallas in Metamorphoses belongs to a male Pallas, not the virgin goddess Athena.
Etias is unattested in the Iliad; Pausanias gives this name to a different figure, so the link is not supported for Iliad Aeneas.
Thrasybulus is unattested as Aeneas's son in the Iliad or Aeneid; it is a doubtful Pausanias-only link.
Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, bore Polypoetes to Odysseus in the Thesprotis epic tradition; this was a union after Troy, not a marriage. Only Penelope is his wife.

The quoted sentence only denies that Aristomenes was a son of Hercules or Zeus. Nicomedes does not appear in it, and the book names no human father in that passage. Wikidata's father link is unconfirmed in this book, so this is probably a misread sentence.

Erytheia is the island where Geryon lived; Pausanias' Erytheia as a daughter is a confusion of place with person. Theoi lists no such child for Geryon, and Hesiod and Apollodorus give him no daughter.
Orthus is Echidna's son (Apollodorus: begotten by Typhon on Echidna); Hesiod's line about Orthus is misread as a union.
Tecmessa was a captive concubine won in war, not a wife; the editor's rule reads non-marriage 'spouse' links as lovers.
Metamorphoses treats Moon as Diana (Artemis); the editor ruled Selene is not Apollo's sibling, so this confuses Selene with Artemis.
The quoted passage calls Caphaurus the grandson of Phoebus; Amphithemis (Garamas) is son of Acacallis and Apollo, but here Caphaurus is the grandson, so the line is misread.
Phialo, daughter of Alcimedon, belongs to the Arcadian Alcimedon of Pausanias (Phigalia legend, mother of Aechmagoras by Heracles), not the Myrmidon son of Laerces in the Iliad.

Pallas as a son of Lycaon comes from Hesiod's tradition and is not in Apollodorus's list of Lycaon's sons; however, Pallas the Arcadian is a different figure (Evander's father), so the link is unsupported here.
Hesiod's Demodoce is a daughter of a different Agenor (the Argive/Pleuron-type figure), not the Phoenician king in Ovid.
Pausanias gives Crotopus as son of the Argive Agenor, son of Triopas, not the Phoenician king.
Iphidamas, son of Antenor in Homer, is confused with Agenor; not a child of the Phoenician king.

Pausanias names Thasus as son of Agenor in some accounts (Phoenician) but the Pausanias link is unclear; the Phoenician Agenor is usually Thasus's father or grandfather, so ambiguous; treat as other Agenor.

link: Theopompus, father of Agenor parent_of Agenor
reasons: This Agenor, son of Theopompus, is a different man from Pausanias, not the Phoenician king.
Preugenes is son of the Achaean Agenor in Pausanias, not the Phoenician king.
Echeclus, son of Agenor, is a Trojan-side figure from a different Agenor, not the Phoenician king.
Dido's father is Belus (Mutto/Belus of Tyre) in Virgil, not Agenor.
Dido's father is Belus (Virgil) or Mattan I (Belus in Aeneid); Agenor is the Phoenician king, father of Cadmus and Europa, and does not fit as Dido's father in Virgil's tradition.

The quoted passage is about Aeneas sailing from Circe's land to the Tiber and says nothing of Faunus. Ovid's Metamorphoses does mention Latinus of Alba Longa, a later king, but that is a different man from the Latinus of the Aeneid.
Ovid's Latinus Silvius is a later Alban king. He is not the Latinus who was king in Latium in the time of Aeneas, and Amata and Lavinia belong to the earlier king.
Enceladus is a Giant, born from Gaia and the blood of Ouranos (Hesiod Theogony 183-187); no source makes Tartarus his father, and Hesiod does not say so.

Hesiod (Theogony 183-185) has the Giants born from Gaia, fertilized by Ouranos' blood; Apollodorus 1.34 names Ouranos and Gaia. Tartarus as father is a rare Typhon-type tradition and is not in Hesiod's account.
Metra is the daughter of Erysichthon, who sold herself to support him (Ovid, Metamorphoses 8), and is not Autolycus' wife. Her link to Autolycus is unsupported.

Autolycus' wife was Neaera in some sources but not Pausanias; Apollodorus gives Amphithea, daughter of Pereus (Apollodorus 1.9.16, 2.4.?). Neaera is a different woman, so this link comes from a confusion.
Adrastus was Polyneikes' father-in-law (Argia's father), not his son; Pausanias' Adrastus is a different relation. Polyneikes' son was Thersander.
In Pausanias, Alpheus only pursued Artemis and failed, and she is a virgin goddess, so he was never her lover. The river is not a partner in the Bacchae.

Anaxiroe is not Epeius's wife in any source I can name; Pausanias has Anaxiroe as daughter of Coronus and wife of Epeius's namesake line is unsupported. The link looks like a confusion with another figure, so it is not a marriage here.
Hyrmina is the daughter of Epeius, son of Endymion, eponym of Hyrmine in Elis; this is a different Epeius from the Trojan horse builder.
Pontus is Gaia's own child, and the Theogony has her bear Nereus, Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto and Eurybia to him. This is a union of mother and son, not a marriage, so it should be read as a lover link.
Hesiod: Gaia bore children to Pontus, but only Uranus is her husband; read as a lover per the editor's rule.
Hesiod's Theia is the Titan sister of Ocean and wife of Hyperion; Apollodorus pairs Ocean only with Tethys, and Hyperion with Thia.

In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Midas's mother is Cybele, whom the Metamorphoses identifies with the Phrygian Great Mother; this is a syncretic link, not a Hesiodic child of Rhea. The Argonautica's Idaean mother is Rhea herself, whose children are the Olympians, and Midas is not one of them.
Apollonius Rhodius 3.1036 makes Hecate daughter of Perses; Zeus as father appears only in a scholiast citing Musaeus, and the book does not tell it.
Hecate is the daughter of Perses and Asteria in Hesiod.

Hesiod's Catalogue (Eugammon's Telegony) has Telegonus, Odysseus' son by Circe, marry Penelope after Odysseus' death. It is a marriage, but only in the Hesiod tradition, and Ovid's Metamorphoses does not tell it, so it should not be kept in this book.
Metamorphoses' Moon is Luna/Selene taken for Diana; the editor ruled Selene unrelated to Apollo.

Ovid's Moon is Selene/Luna, not Diana; the editor ruled Selene is not Apollo's sibling or relative.

Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus, wife of Castor; not Apollo's child.
Lycomedes is not Apollo's son in Pausanias; likely confusion with another Lycomedes.
Hesione was a Trojan captive given to Telamon as war prize (concubine), mother of Teucer in some accounts; not a wife by the editor's rule.
A chorus is a group in Aeschylus' play, not a person; the individual Oceanids are his children.
Hesiod makes Theia a Titan sister who marries Hyperion; she is also listed as an Oceanid, but never as Oceanus' wife. His wife is Tethys.
The river Xanthus (Scamander) is a Trojan river god. The editor's Midas parent of Xanthus note concerns a different Xanthus, so the link may confuse two figures.
Passalus is a Cercopes figure, and the link looks like a confusion with Oceanus' children. Hesiod does not make him Oceanus' son.
Acmon is a Cercopes name or a Dactyl. The link looks like a confusion with the Oceanid in Hesiod.
Pausanias' Ætolus son of Oxylus (brother of Laias) is a different, later Ætolus from Endymion's son, the eponym of Aetolia.
Pausanias calls Dipoinos and Skyllis pupils of Daedalus (Cretan tradition), not his sons; Dipoinos is not his child in Metamorphoses or the Theoi listing.

Hermus is a river, a son of Okeanos and Tethys in Hesiod, not a child of Zeus.
Eetion in Hesiod is Iasion's variant name, not a son of Zeus; here it confuses the two.
Pausanias gives the Sibyl as a daughter of Zeus and Lamia in some accounts, but the editor accepts the Lamia and Theodorus parentage only in pausanias, so it should not be in this book.
Opportunity (Kairos) as son of Zeus is only a Pausanias personification and is not used in Pindar.

Pandora was a gift to Epimetheus; Hesiod does not make her Zeus's lover.
Vulcan is the Roman Hephaistos; this is a Roman-name duplicate.

The book's Hesiod passage makes Anaxibia a child of Pleisthenes and Cleolla, so she is Atreus's granddaughter. The Wikidata link skips a generation (the other tradition, in which Anaxibia is Atreus's daughter, is not told in this book).
Hyperion is not a child of Agamemnon; Pausanias names Hyperion as a son of Aegisthus's era? No: he is a son of Orestes' line or a Titan namesake, so the link confuses two beings.
A group label, not a person; Pausanias names Medeus and Eriopis (Cinaethon) and Mermerus and Pheres elsewhere, so the collective link is redundant.

link: Aegyptus parent_of Chorus of the Danaids
reasons: The Chorus of the Danaids are the daughters of Danaus, not of Aegyptus; Aegyptus fathered the fifty sons who pursued them.
Erytheia is the island where Geryon lived. Pausanias' Erythea (a Hesperid nymph) is not his child, and Theoi lists no such child for Geryon.
Pausanias' Polydamas, son of Nicias, is the huge Thessalian athlete of Skotoussa, not a child of the Athenian general Nicias, so the link belongs to a different Nicias.
Pausanias' Polydamas son of Nicias is the Scotussan athlete, a different man from Hector's friend (son of Panthous).
Metra is the daughter of Erysichthon, wife of Autolycus' namesake line? Actually no source gives Autolycus a wife Metra; Metamorphoses has no such marriage, so the link is a misread.
Endeis, mother of Peleus and wife of Aiakos, was daughter of Cheiron, not a Nereid; the Pausanias link confuses her with a Nereid sister of Thetis, and Theoi lists her as no Nereid.
Pisus in Pausanias is a different figure (son of Perieres of Elis-line tradition); Apollodorus does not give Perieres this son, and Pausanias' Pisus is a separate figure.

Nicostratus is the son of Menelaus by a slave woman (Pieris the Aetolian or Tereis), not Helen; Apollodorus' Epitome gives Helen only Hermione, and in Hesiod Nicostratus is a son of Menelaus by another mother.

Duplicate spelling of Iphicles, who is already linked from the book's own sentence.

Spelling duplicate of Tlepolemus.

In Hesiod's Theogony, Eros arises on his own beside Earth and Tartarus; Chaos is not his parent. Theoi's note does not support this link in this book.
Hesiod's Theogony (116-122) names Eros as born at the start alongside Chaos, Gaia and Tartarus, with no parent. Chaos as his father comes from Oppian and Orphic-style sources, not Hesiod.
Hesiod (Theogony 116) has Chaos come first, with no parents. Chronos as parent is from the Orphic tradition, which this book does not follow.
Hesiod's Theogony (116) has Chaos come into being first, with no parent; the Orphic Chronos (time) is a different figure from the Titan Cronus and is not Chaos's father in Hesiod.
Paris took Helen to Troy; the editor's rule reads every spouse link other than the marriage to Menelaus as a lover, and Menelaus is her husband.

The union with Achilles on the White Island is a post-death tradition (Pausanias), not a marriage, so it is a lover link.
Helen and Achilles are joined only in a late afterlife tradition (Pausanias); the Aeneid has no marriage, so under the editor's rule it is at most a lover link.
Lucina is a title of Juno (or Diana) as birth goddess, not a daughter of Ops; the link rests on a cult title taken for a person.

Lucina is a cult title of Juno (or Diana), not a separate daughter of Ops; Ovid's Ilithyia is Juno's birth-goddess aspect, whose mother would be Rhea/Ops only as Juno's mother, so the link confuses a title with a person.

Pausanias (Hermione) calls Clymenus a Hermionian, a son of Phoroneus or Foroneus who founded a Demeter cult. He is not a sibling of Demeter, so this confuses a cult title or founder with a god. Hades as Clymenus is a separate epithet, so the link is unsupported.

Despoina is the Arcadian cult title of Persephone, so Despœna is the same being as Persephone and not a second child. Pausanias (8.37) says she is Demeter's daughter by Poseidon, which makes her a separate cult figure there. She duplicates the Persephone link.

In the Aeneid Pilumnus is Turnus's grandsire (his ancestor), not Venilia's husband. Virgil names Daunus as Turnus's father (10.616). Pilumnus is also Daunus's ancestor, so this link confuses the generations.
In Aeneid 10.76 Venilia is Turnus's mother and the wife of Daunus, not of Pilumnus. Pilumnus is Turnus's ancestor (Aeneid 9.4, 10.619), so the link confuses him with Daunus.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses (14.332) Canens is the daughter of Janus and Venilia. The Aeneid says nothing of this, and the link is from another book and shouldn't be here.

In Ovid's Metamorphoses 14, Vertumnus, disguised as an old woman, persuades Pomona and then wins her; they are united as a couple, and Wikidata lists him as her spouse. The quoted sentence only shows his rivalry as a suitor.
Apollodorus 3.6.4 means the Lycurgus king of Nemea, husband of Eurydice, not the Thracian king; Opheltes belongs to the Nemean Lycurgus.
Aleus's son Lycurgus is the Arcadian of Tegea, not the Thracian king; the editor holds it right for this book, so it belongs to the Arcadian Lycurgus.
Apollodorus 3.9.2 gives Iasus to the Arcadian Lycurgus, son of Aleus, not the Thracian.
Apollodorus 3.9.2 gives Amphidamas to the Arcadian Lycurgus, son of Aleus, not the Thracian.

Neither Theoi nor Wikidata names Iapetus as Lucifer's father. The tradition gives Astraeus or Cephalus with Eos (Aurora), and Iapetus is Atlas's father, so this looks like a confusion with Atlas.
Deidameia bore Neoptolemos to Achilles on Skyros but was not his wife in the main tradition; the editor's rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lover.
Helen and Achilles joined only in the afterlife on Leuke (Pausanias); this was no marriage on earth, so lover is the fit.
Hesiod's Homeric Hymn tradition has Hermes lie with Dryops' daughter; no marriage, so per editor's rule this is a lover.
Pindar's 'Fame' is a personified abstraction, not a child of Hermes.
Faunus is the Roman woodland god, son of Picus; the Hermes-Pan/Faunus link rests on a conflation of Faunus with Pan.

Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, is a different figure; Dione is her mother only in a Hyginus-type tradition that is not the Iliad's, and it is a later confusion (Dione as Atlantid) that this book does not tell.
Pasithea is the wife of Hypnos (Sleep) in Homer (Iliad 14) and Nonnus; Pausanias' line calls her only his beloved, but the tradition makes her his wife.

Sicyon is the son of Marathon (Pausanias 2.6.5) or Metion's line in some accounts; Hesiod's Sicyon link is not as a child of Erechtheus. Pausanias also gives Sicyon's father as Erechtheus' descendant in a variant, but the main tradition does not make him Erechtheus' son.
The Doliones are a people, not a person; their eponym Dolion was a son of Silene or Poseidon, not the group itself.

Book's Moon is Diana/Luna as Apollo's sister, but the editor says Selene is not Apollo's child; the link confuses Selene with Diana.
Apis son of Apollo in Aeschylus is a seer of Argos, not connected to this book's tradition; likely a different Apis, but unconfirmed by Theoi.
Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus (wife of Castor), not Apollo's child.
Pycimede is Ileus's daughter-line figure, not Apollo's child in the cited tradition.

Erytheia is the island where Geryon lived (Hesiod: 'Erytheia'), not his child; the other book's Erythea as a daughter appears to confuse the place or a nymph of that name with a child of Geryon.

The boy boxer Hellanicus, son of Alcaenetus, in the 89th Olympiad is a different man from the historian Hellanicus of Mytilene.

Deidameia bore Neoptolemus to Achilles on Scyros, but the tradition describes a union, not a marriage; editor rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lover.

The union of Achilles and Helen on Leuce is a late posthumous tale (Pausanias), not a marriage in the Iliad; lover at most.
Boreas carried Orithyia off by force (Apollodorus 3.15.2), and the editor's rule reads any spouse link other than a marriage as a lover.

Direction reversed: Pandora is Pyrrha's mother, not her daughter (Apollodorus 1.7.2 makes Pyrrha the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora).
Thyia, mother of Magnes and Macedon by Zeus in Hesiod's Catalogue, is the daughter of Deucalion, not of Pyrrha; the Wikidata link confuses her with another figure.
Amphissos by Apollo belongs to Dryope daughter of Eurytus/Dryops in Ovid; here the hymn's Dryops' daughter is Pan's mother by Hermes, a different Dryope.
Andraemon married Ovid's Dryope, Iole's half-sister; this is not Hermes' bride in the Hymn to Pan.
Iole is half-sister of Ovid's Dryope (daughter of Eurytus), not the nymph bride of Hermes.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses the Iole who is sister of Dryope (daughter of Dryops) is the wife of Thoas, a different woman from Eurytus' daughter Iole of Oechalia.

Iambe's usual parentage is Pan and Echo in some sources (Pan and Echo), but Hesiod doesn't mention this and Iambe is a Demeter-hymn servant; however the Pan–Echo tradition does exist, so this is uncertain.
The Hesiod (Catalogue of Women) Antiope is a daughter of the son of Nauboius (Phocian line, mother of Iolea, Minyan context), not the Amazon Antiope, daughter of Ares.

Ares fathered the Amazon Antiope (Pausanias, Theoi), but Hesiod's Antiope is the daughter of Nauboius's grandson/son, so the link belongs to the Amazon.

Apollodorus' Erigone is the daughter of Icarius of Athens, not Icarus, the son of Daedalus. The Metamorphoses link confuses the similar names Icarius and Icarus.
Astraea as Helen's mother confuses a namesake; the standard mothers are Leda or Nemesis, not Astraea.

Helen was abducted by Theseus as a girl and never married to him; she was only a captive or lover.

Achilles and Helen as a pair belong to the afterlife tradition on Leuke (Pausanias), not a marriage in this book; read as lover.
Ixion's father is usually Phlegyas (also Antion, Peision, or Leonteus in other sources); Ares as father is an unsupported outlier from Wikidata, not stated in Aeschylus.
Ixion's father is Phlegyas (or Antion/Peision), not Ares; Ares is the father of Phlegyas, so Ixion is a grandson at most.
Dryope was Hermes' lover (mother of Pan in the Homeric Hymn); the editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.
Hesiod's Dryope, mother of Pan by Hermes, is a different nymph; Ovid's Dryope bore Amphissus to Apollo and married Andraemon.

Themistonoe belongs to a different Cycnus, the Hesiodic one is the son of Ares; the Themistonoe link is to the Cycnus of Colonae, so this is a namesake.
Hemithea and Tennes are children of Cycnus king of Colonae (son of Poseidon), not Ares' son killed by Heracles.
Tennes is the son of Cycnus of Tenedos/Colonae, a different man from Ares' son.
Phylonome is the wife of Cycnus of Colonae in Pausanias, not Ares' son.
Pirithous was son of Ixion (or Zeus) and Dia; Aethra is Theseus' mother, and Apollodorus gives Pirithous no link to her.
Aethra is Theseus' mother; Pirithous' mother is Dia (wife of Ixion), so this confuses him with his friend Theseus.
Pausanias' Aethra wife of Phalanthus of Taras is a different woman, not Theseus' mother; Apollodorus does not mention this.

Apollodorus gives no parentage for Nephele; the Oceanid parentage is not stated in this book, and the Wikipedia entry notes two Nepheles, so this is not clearly attached to the Athamas wife. Not contradicted by a source, though, so cautious removal is not warranted.
Nessus the centaur is the son of Ixion and the cloud Nephele (the Ixion cloud). Apollodorus' Nephele, mother of Phrixus and Helle, is the other figure, so the link joins two beings.

The Iliad's Chryses is the Trojan priest of Apollo. Minos was the father of a different Chryses, the son of Minos and Paria, who appears in the Parian/Cretan tradition. Wikidata's father list (Ardys, Minos) shows the two are mixed up.
Chryses son of Minos (by Paria) is a Wikidata-only link; in the Iliad Chryses is Apollo's priest, a different person, and no source here supports it.

Phineus is Cepheus's brother, Andromeda's uncle and fiancé in Ovid, not Cassiope's son; the Hesiod-derived link appears to confuse him with another Phineus.
Glaucon the Athenian victor is son of Eteocles of Athens/Orchomenos (Andreus's son), not the Theban son of Oedipus.
Pausanias's Eteocles son of Andreus (Orchomenian, said son of Cephisus) is a different man from the Theban son of Oedipus.
Phialo, mother of Aechmis by Heracles, was the daughter of the Arcadian Alcimedon in Pausanias. Ovid's Alcimedon is a different man, a sailor in Acoetes' crew in Metamorphoses 3.

Aethra lay with Ægeus (and Poseidon) in one night at Troezen; she was not his wife in the tradition, so mark as lover.
Laestrygon as Poseidon's son is a tradition only in Hesiod's lost fragments; hard to support, but Telepylus founder Lamus is the usual source. Weak, but not contradicted.
Machaon is son of Asclepius, not Poseidon.
Podaleirius is son of Asclepius, not Poseidon.

Megarian Alcathous is son of Pelops and Hippodamia (Pausanias 1.41, Wikidata); Porthaon's son Alcathous is a different man, so the link mixes two namesakes.

Thespius is Apollodorus' king of Thespiae, father of the fifty daughters, not a son of Erechtheus; Wikidata mixes him up with another figure.
