Hesiod (Theogony 901) calls Themis Zeus's second wife, and Wikidata lists Zeus as her spouse. The editor's rule reads only Hera/Juno as Zeus's marriages, but Themis is not listed there, so lover is too weak; she is a wife.
Themis was Zeus's wife according to Hesiod.
Editor's decision: Aratus is Asklepios's child only in pausanias (where he is a mortal son of Clinias and Aristodama in Sicyon), so the link does not hold for this book.
In Pausanias, Alpheus pursued Artemis but never won her. She is a virgin goddess, so he is not her lover; she escaped him (Arethusa's story is a separate myth). Oedipus the King does not mention it.
Apollodorus gives Arcas as Callisto's son and never names her as Pan's mother. The editor has ruled that Dryops' daughter is Pan's mother, and only in Hesiod.
Apollodorus lists Europa, Cadmus, Phoenix and Cilix as the children of Agenor and Telephassa; Thasus is not among them, and the book elsewhere treats him as a son or companion of Cilix or Phoenix.
Apollodorus names Phineus as a son of Agenor (or Poseidon) in a different passage, not by Telephassa; the book lists only four children of Telephassa.
Nero was Claudius's stepson and adoptive son, not his biological child; Claudius's children were Octavia and Britannicus, and Nero's father was Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus.

link: Hermione spouse_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
reasons: Pyrrhus is another name for Neoptolemus, so this duplicates the Neoptolemus link; keep one marriage and drop the duplicate node.

link: Lysimachus parent_of Alexander, son of Cassander
reasons: Pausanias says Alexander was Lysimachus' son by Odrysiades; Alexander son of Cassander is a different man, so the link confuses two people.
Ascanius is Aeneas's son by Creusa (Metamorphoses 14 calls him Iulus, son of Aeneas); Lavinia is his stepmother. Her son was Silvius in some traditions (Virgil, Aeneid 6).

In the standard tradition Ascanius (Iulus) is the son of Aeneas and Creusa; Lavinia is his stepmother (in Livy she bears Silvius, and in some versions Ascanius is her son, but Ovid's Metamorphoses does not say so).
Editor ruled Cronus parent of Crius wrong everywhere; Crius was Cronus's brother, a Titan.
Crius was a son of Uranus and Gaia (Hesiod, Theogony); the editor has ruled Cronus as parent of Crius wrong everywhere.
Picus is the Latin king of Virgil and Ovid, son of Saturn in Latin tradition. Theoi's Cronos listing does not make him a child of the Greek Cronos in Pausanias.
Hesiod gives the Moirai as daughters of Night (Theogony 217), and in other versions of Zeus and Themis. Cronus is not their father.

Pausanias (Hermione) makes Clymenus a Chthonian god or an Argive figure honoured as Hades, and a local Hermionean tradition makes him Demeter's brother-in-cult. In Pindar the family is Kronos and Rhea's children, so he is not a sibling here.

In the Iliad Hera only promises Hypnos that Pasithea will be his wife; she is not Hera's daughter. Pausanias gives Pasithea as a Charis or a daughter of Aegle, and Theoi's listing does not make her Hera's child.
Andromeda's mother is Cassiopeia, wife of Cepheus, queen of Aethiopia. Hesiod's Cassiopea is the wife of Phoenix and mother of Phineus, so the Andromeda link belongs to the other Cassiopeia.
Iole is daughter of Eurytus of Oechalia, but Pausanias' Eurytus is the Molionid son of Actor (father of Thalpius), a different man.
Antioche is the wife of Eurytus of Oechalia in Hesiod; Pausanias gives this Eurytus wife Theraphone.
Hesiod makes Theia a Titan sister who bore Helios, Selene and Eos to Hyperion; Ocean's wife is Tethys.
A chorus is a group, not a person; the Oceanids are already linked individually.
Triptolemus is son of Celeus and Metaneira (or Eleusis); the Ocean/Gaia parentage is a rare variant not found in this book.
The Cercopes are a pair of brigands, a group, not an individual child; the Ocean parentage is unsupported.
Acmon is a Titan figure in Hesiod's tradition and not truly Ocean's child; the link is an unsupported guess.
Euryphaessa is Hyperion's wife (a variant of Theia) in the tradition, not his sister as a separate sibling link; the sibling link double counts the relationship.
Pasithea is a Grace (Charis) in Hesiod, daughter of Zeus and Eurynome; the Iliad's Hera only promises Hypnos a Grace as a bride, so she is not Pasithea's mother.

Hesiod's Sicyon is a son of Erechtheus only in a rare tradition (Pausanias says Marathon's son; Sicyon is eponym of Sicyon, son of Metion in Pausanias); not in Apollodorus' list of Erechtheus' children.
Orneus is son of Erechtheus in Pausanias, but Apollodorus lists Cecrops, Pandorus and Metion as sons; Orneus is better read as a link from Pausanias' tradition, a variant not in this book.
Hesiod's Dryops' daughter bore Pan to Hermes but was not a wife; only marriages count as spouse, so read as a lover.
Pindar's Fame (Angelia, a personification) is not a child of Hermes in Pausanias; this is a misread of the herald's role.
Apollodorus 1.2.7 says the Nereids were born to Nereus and Doris, so Doris is his wife and not his child. The link reverses the relationship, and the spouse link already covers it.
Afterlife union on Leuce reported by a visionary, not a marriage; treated as a lover under the editor's rule.
Most sources (Homeric Hymn 19, Herodotus, Apollodorus, Plato) make Hermes Pan's father; Zeus as father is a rare variant that the book's text does not state.

Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, bore Polypoetes to Odysseus after his return (Eugammon's Telegony) and is not a marriage like Penelope's; under the editor's rule that only marriages count, a second spouse is read as a lover.
Pausanias (5.7.4, 6.22.9) tells of Alpheus pursuing Artemis, who tricked him, so no lover relationship. Artemis was a virgin goddess and Alpheus's love for Arethusa is the better-known tale.
Doris is Nereus' wife and the mother of his daughters; Apollodorus lists her among the Oceanids, daughters of Oceanus and Tethys, not of Nereus.
Cyanippus was the son of Aegialeus's sister Deipyle and Tydeus's... no: Cyanippus was son of Aegialeus per Pausanias only, while Apollodorus makes Cyanippus son of Aegeus's... he is son of Adrastus.
Apollodorus 3.5.6 names Amphion's wife Niobe as daughter of Tantalus, a different Niobe from Phoroneus' daughter; Amphion and her children belong to the Theban Niobe.
Chloris, daughter of Amphion and Niobe, belongs to the Theban Niobe, not Phoroneus' daughter.
Hesiod makes the Graces daughters of Zeus and Eurynome; Pindar does not name Aphrodite as their mother.
Iliad has Zeus as father of both, but Ares' mother is Hera and Aphrodite's is Dione, so they are half-siblings at best; the link is misleading and the usual tradition makes them lovers.
Iliad makes Aphrodite daughter of Zeus and Dione, not Hera, so she is only half-sister at most; the standard tradition makes her Ares' lover, not sibling.
Hesiod's Clymene, wife of Phylacus (mother of Iphiclus), is a daughter of Minyas, not Ovid's Clymene, mother of Phaëton and wife of Merops.

link: Clymene parent_of Iphiclus, son of Phylacus
reasons: Iphiclus's mother in Hesiod is the Minyan Clymene, a different woman from the Oceanid who is Phaëton's mother.
Iapetus's wife is the Oceanid Clymene of Hesiod, but Ovid's Clymene is Phaëton's mother, married to Merops. The two are conflated under one name.
Doris is Nereus's wife, not his daughter; Hesiod makes her daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, and she is the mother of the Nereids by Nereus.
Pausanias' Oeolycus is an ancestor of the Aegeidae of Sparta, a different Aegeus; Athenian Aegeus is the son of Pandion.

Pausanias (7.4) gives Ancaeus and Samia the children Perilaus, Enudus, Samos, Alitherses and Parthenope. However, this Parthenope is Ancaeus' daughter, mother of Lycomedes by Apollo; the link fits only if it is this Parthenope, so it is likely correct and should be kept.
Harmonia was Ares' daughter by Aphrodite, and married Cadmus; Ares was only a lover of Aphrodite, and the editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lover links.
Hermes is a half-brother only via Zeus, which is a loose kinship from Statius; the sibling link is unsupported by the tree's own parents.

link: Ares parent_of Melanippus, son of Ares
reasons: Pausanias names a Melanippus only as a son of Ares in a minor tale; the entry looks like a placeholder-named figure and cannot be confirmed.
Panic is a personification, not a person; Phobos and Deimos are the sons.
Deidameia bore Neoptolemus to Achilles on Scyros, but the tradition (Hesiod, Apollodorus) treats this as a union without formal marriage, so it is read as a lover per the editor's rule.

link: Achilles parent_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
reasons: Pyrrhus is another name for Neoptolemus, so this duplicates the Neoptolemus link; it should be merged into one entry, not kept as a separate child.

Hesiod (Theogony 326-327) makes Orthos and Chimaera the parents of the Nemean lion (Phix and the lion). Typhoeus as father comes from Apollodorus, not Hesiod, so it does not belong in this book's tree.
In the Aeneid Misenus is the son of Aeolus, a Trojan, not the keeper of the winds, Hippotes' son; these are different men named Aeolus.
Minyas' father in the Argonautica tradition is a different Aeolus, not Hippotes' son the wind-keeper (Minyas is usually son of Orchomenus, Poseidon or Chryses).
Lathria belongs to a different Aristodemus in Pausanias (the Messenian king, or another namesake), not the Heraclid husband of Argia.
Anaxandra is a wife of another Aristodemus in Pausanias (the Messenian king's circle), not the Heraclid.
The daughter belongs to the Messenian king Aristodemus (sacrificed daughter), not the Heraclid, whose children are Eurysthenes and Procles.
Duplicate of the Messenian Aristodemus's daughter; not the Heraclid's child.
Artylas is father of a different Aristodemus; Apollodorus and Wikidata make Aristomachus the Heraclid's father.

Telemachus marries Circe in the Telegony epic cycle. Hesiod's Theogony 1011-16 and the Odyssey do not say so; the book lists only a lover relationship with Odysseus. The Wikidata spouse is the Telegony version. The editor's rule reads spouse links as lovers, so keep it as a lover link.
A group node duplicating the individual sons Polynices and Eteocles, who are already linked as his children.
Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.453 makes the Furies daughters of Night, so Earth and Uranus (Hesiod's tradition) are not this book's parentage.
Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.453 makes the Furies daughters of Night, so Earth and Uranus (Hesiod's tradition) are not this book's parentage.
Pausanias' Aratus is the Sicyonian statesman, son of Clinias and Aristodama (editor's decision), not a child of Asclepius.

In Metamorphoses, 'Pallas' and 'Tritonia' here is Minerva (Athena), daughter of Jupiter; the Wikidata Pallas is the friend of Athena, daughter of Triton, so the Jupiter link is right only for the goddess.
Pallas here is Minerva's epithet or a Titan Pallas, not Jupiter's own child apart from Minerva.
The Pallas who is father of Clytus and Butes is the Athenian Pallas, brother of Aegeus (Metamorphoses 7), not the goddess or Triton's daughter.
The Pallas who is father of Clytus and Butes is the Athenian Pallas, brother of Aegeus (Metamorphoses 7), not the goddess or Triton's daughter.

The book's sentence names Artemisia, wife of Mausolus, who is Artemisia II of Caria (4th century BC). The Wikidata match is Artemisia I, fl. 480 BC, daughter of Lygdamis I, so the link belongs to a different woman.
Dido's brother in the Aeneid is Pygmalion of Tyre, the king who murdered Sychaeus; Ovid's Pygmalion is a sculptor-king of Cyprus, a different person.

link: Arcas parent_of Pelasgus, son of Arcas
reasons: Pausanias makes Pelasgus the father of Lycaon and so Arcas's ancestor, not his son; the link confuses two figures, and the name 'son of Arcas' looks like a misread.
Pausanias' Aratus is the Sicyonian statesman, son of Clinias and Aristodama (editor's decision), not a child of Asclepius.
In the Aeneid, Alcanor of Mount Ida is the father of the Trojan brothers Pandarus and Bitias, who are a different Pandarus. The Iliad's Pandarus is the Lycian archer, son of Lycaon.
Bitias is the brother of the Aeneid's Pandarus, son of Alcanor. The Iliad's Pandarus, son of Lycaon, has no such brother.
A chorus is a group, not a person; the Oceanids are already her daughters individually.
The river Xanthus in Hesiod's list is a son of Ocean and Tethys; the Midas-related Xanthus is another figure, but the editor's decision on Midas stands.

Pausanias (2.16.1) makes Sthenelus the son of Crotopus's descendant line, not of Crotopus; in Pausanias Crotopus's son is Sthenelas per some accounts, but Statius's Thebaid (1.557-668) names only Psamathe and Linus as his children, so this link is an unsupported import.
Hesiod (Theogony 225) makes Night alone bear Strife, with no father; Erebus is not named as her parent in this book.
In Hesiod's Theogony (211-225), Strife (Eris) is a child of Night alone, and Sleep likewise; Erebus is not named as their father.
Pasithea is a Grace; in Homer (Iliad 14) Hera promises her to Sleep as a bride, and she is not Hera's daughter. Theoi's listing is not a good basis, and the editor rejects other parentage for her.
Enyo is Ares' companion; in the Iliad she is a war goddess, and her parentage as Hera's daughter is a late, unsupported guess here.
Pausanias' Electra daughter of Atlas (the Pleiad, mother of Dardanus) is a different person from Agamemnon's daughter; the tree mixes two Electras.
Electra sister of Cadmus (Electran gate at Thebes) is a different person from Agamemnon's daughter.
Iliad 11.248 makes Coon Antenor's son, but not Theano's; Homer gives a different mother (Coon is Antenor's son by a different woman in tradition), so the Wikidata link is unsupported.
Helicaon is Antenor's son (Iliad 3.123) by Laodice's marriage, not Theano's; the Wikidata link is unsupported.
Ceryx is the son of Hermes and Agraulus, daughter of Cecrops (Pausanias), not Cecrops' wife, the daughter of Actaeus.
Apollodorus 3.14.2 makes Cecrops' daughter Agraulus a different person from his wife Agraulus, daughter of Actaeus.

Apollodorus 3.14.2 names Agraulus as Cecrops' wife and also as a daughter; the daughter link imported from Pausanias duplicates the daughter Aglauros, already linked from Metamorphoses, and splits one daughter into two entries.
Ovid's Metamorphoses has Nyctimene as daughter of Epopeus of Lesbos, not Nycteus; the tradition giving Nycteus a daughter Nyctimene is a different one and is not what Pausanias says.
Epimedes is one of the Idaean Dactyls named in Pausanias (5.7.6), not a sibling; the link treats a member of the group as a separate sibling.
Arete is Alcinous' wife and niece (daughter of his brother Rhexenor), not his sibling; the Argonautica calls her his wife.
Pausanias' Troilus is not a son of Alcinous of Phaeacia; this link comes from a namesake or misreading.
Alcetus belongs to a different Alcinous in Pausanias, not the Phaeacian king.
Galanthis is Alcmene's servant in Metamorphoses 9, not Tiresias's daughter; Pausanias does not make her his child.

Ovid (Met. 9) makes Galanthis a servant of Alcmena, with no father named; Tiresias is not her father. Antoninus Liberalis gives Galinthias as daughter of Proetus of Thebes, and the link from Pausanias looks like a mix-up with Tiresias' daughter Manto.

Iphigenia's mother is Clytemnestra (Wikidata, Aeschylus, Euripides); Helen is Clytemnestra's sister and Hermione's mother. Only a rare tradition (Stesichorus, in Pausanias) makes Helen the mother, and this book does not tell it.
Dirce was the wife of Lycus, not Antiope's child; she was Antiope's tormentor, so this link is a mistake.
Pausanias says Dirce defamed Antiope and was killed by Antiope's sons, so Antiope is her victim and enemy, not her mother.
This is the Amazon Antiope, sister of Hippolyta, taken by Theseus; the Theban Antiope is a different person.
Hippolyta's sister is the Amazon Antiope, not the Theban daughter of Nycteus or Asopus.
No ancient source makes Hecate the mother of Janus; Metamorphoses 14 only gives Janus as father of Canens by Venilia, and the Wikidata mother is a doubtful later guess.
Janus is a Roman god with no tradition of Hecate as his mother; no ancient source supports this link, which confuses unrelated beings.

Wikidata's Caelus is the Roman Uranus, but the book never says this, and Janus's parents are given elsewhere as Caelus and Hecate or as Saturn, so the link is a doubtful identification, not the book's own tradition.
Pausanias calls Sisyphus 'the son of Aeolus'; Zeus is not his father in the book or in the tradition (Aeolus and Enarete).
Sisyphus is a son of Aeolus.
Aidos is not Prometheus' child in Hesiod; Theoi's confirmation seems to stem from a misread. Hesiod has Aidos only as a personified goddess without that parentage.
Selene is not Apollo's sister. The editor ruled that Selene-Apollo links are wrong; Diana is the sister, and the Moon here is a confusion (Metamorphoses).
Scylla's parentage is Phorcys/Crataeis or Triton, not Apollo; this is an unsupported guess, and Hesiod is dubious here.
Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus, not Apollo; she was a Leucippid, wife of Castor.
Hesiod's Phaethon, son of Eos and Cephalus, is a different being from Ovid's Phaethon, son of Clymene and the Sun; the editor ruled Cephalus as parent only right in Pausanias.

Pausanias 10.6 has Poseidon's intrigue with Thyia, but that is a different Thyia (Cephissus' daughter, in Pausanias' Delphic context, mother of Chloris' circle); the link mixes two namesakes. Actually the Poseidon passage in 9.36 concerns Chloris and Neleus, not Deucalion's daughter.
Harmonia is Ares' daughter. The Argonautica link misreads the family, and Harmonia married Cadmus.
Duplicate of the Penthesileia node, which is the same Amazon queen.
Thestius is the son of Agenor or Ares in some sources; Theoi lists him as Ares' son but other sources make him a son of Ares only in rare traditions. This may not be the same Thestius the book names.
Pausanias (citing Areus) makes Thestius son of Agenor, grandson of Pleuron; Ares and Aphrodite as parents look like a confusion with another figure, not this Thestius.
Melanippe is an Amazon, usually the daughter of Ares only in some sources, and the Argonautica reading is a guess at a different Melanippe.
Hesiod's Theogony makes Echidna Typhon's mate, and Wikidata lists her as his spouse. This is a union, not a casual affair.

The Iliad (13.450-452) makes Deucalion his father and Minos his grandfather; Minos as father comes from Pausanias and conflicts with this book's tree, since Minos parent of Deucalion is the editor's accepted link.
Paris carried Helen off to Troy and the editor reads any non-marriage 'spouse' link as a lover. The Iliad does treat her as his wife at Troy, but the editor's rule is final.
Pausanias tells of a posthumous union on Leuke, which is not a marriage; at most a lover.
Theseus abducted the young Helen; there was no marriage, so he counts as a lover.
Theseus abducted the child Helen but did not marry her; she was rescued by the Dioscuri.
Wikidata lists Selene as Endymion's spouse, and in the tradition she bore him fifty daughters (Pausanias 5.1.4), so she is more than a lover.
Duplicate spelling of Tleptolemus, the same son; keep only the book's Tleptolemus form.
Duplicate spelling of Tleptolemus, the same son.
Aventinus is a Roman tradition from the Aeneid, not Pausanias; a different tradition but not contradicted, though the link is off-topic here.
Duplicate spelling of Iphicles, already linked.

link: Hercules sibling_of Iphiclus, son of Amphitryon
reasons: Duplicate spelling of Iphicles, already linked.

link: Hercules parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
reasons: A group taken for a person; the sons by Megara are not a single individual.
Helen and Achilles were united only after death on Leuke (Pausanias, Ptolemy Hephaestion); the editor's rule reads any spouse other than a marriage as a lover.
Achilles and Helen's union on Leuke is a late tale of an afterlife pairing, not a marriage; the editor treats non-marriages as lover links.

link: Achilles parent_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
reasons: Pyrrhus is another name of Neoptolemus, Achilles' son, already listed; the entry for the later king of Epirus is a different person and duplicates the link.
Agesipolis and Cleombrotus were sons of King Pausanias, son of Pleistoanax and exiled c. 395 BC, not of the regent of Plataea who was Pleistoanax's father.
Oenopion is son of Dionysus and Ariadne (Apollodorus Epitome); Wikidata's Theseus link is a confusion with Ariadne's children by Theseus in some traditions, not in this book.
Hesiod (via Plutarch) names Aegle as Theseus's passion for whom he abandoned Ariadne; a lover, not a wife.
Hippolyte is the Amazon, equated with Antiope; Apollodorus has Theseus carry off an Amazon, mother of Hippolytus, not marry her formally. Treated as a lover.
In Apollodorus, Theseus carries off the Amazon (Antiope or Hippolyte) and has Hippolytus by her; the link comes from Statius, and by the editor's rule non-marriage links are read as lovers.

link: Theseus parent_of Iphigenia, daughter of Theseus
reasons: Pausanias's Iphigenia, daughter of Theseus and Helen, is a minor tradition and is not named in Apollodorus; she is not Agamemnon's Iphigenia.

link: Theseus parent_of Melanippus, son of Theseus
reasons: Pausanias-only figure, not in Apollodorus, easily confused with other Melanippi.
Aeschylus's Argus is not Earth's child here; Apollodorus gives Argus Panoptes as son of Arestor or as earth-born, a different being.
Midas is the Phrygian king in Ovid's Metamorphoses, not a child of the Titan Rhea (possibly confused with Cybele); Hesiod never says this.
In the Odyssey, Nestor's wife is a different Eurydice (daughter of Clymenus), not Orpheus' wife the nymph.
Apollodorus 3.6.4 names Opheltes' mother as Eurydice, wife of Lycurgus of Nemea, a different person from Orpheus' wife.

The book has Aethra say Aegeus wedded her, but the editor's rule reads any spouse link beyond marriages as a lover; Aethra's union with Aegeus was a single night in Troezen, so it is better recorded as a lover link.

In the Aeneid Hyrtacus is the father of Nisus. Hippocoon son of Hyrtacus is a Trojan in the Aeneid's Sicilian games (Hippocoon, Hyrtacides, Aen. 5.492), so the link is likely right, though Hyrtacus of Arisbe is a different person from the Trojan in the Iliad.
Endeis, wife of Aeacus and mother of Peleus, is a daughter of Chiron (or Skiron), not a Nereid. She is no sister of Thetis; the link likely confuses her with Peleus's family.

Apollodorus' Demophon, the child nursed by Demeter, is the son of Metanira and Celeus of Eleusis. He is not the Thracian king of Elaeus in the Wikipedia description, and the match should be fixed, but this parent link is right for the book's Demophon.
Theseus' son Demophon (Phaedra's son, Acamas' brother) is a different person from Celeus' son at Eleusis. The link comes from other books, not this one's Demophon.

Boreas is son of Astraeus and Eos in Hesiod's Theogony (Theoi lists Astraeus and Eos as parents of the winds), so this is actually right; but Hesiod names Boreas, Zephyrus, Notus as children of Astraeus and Eos, so keep.
Actor is Moline's husband, not her child; the Molionides are Eurytus and Cteatus, sons of Actor (or Poseidon) and Moline. Wikidata lists Actor as her spouse.
Pausanias says this Mæra's father was Prœtus son of Thersander, grandson of Sisyphus (Nostoi), a different Prœtus from the son of Abas.

Anaxilas of Rhegium was the son of Cretines (per Wikipedia); Pausanias (4.23) says he descended from Alcidamidas, who fled Messenia after the Spartan conquest, so he is a distant descendant, not a son.
Peleus' wife Antigone in Apollodorus is the daughter of Eurytion (or of Actor), a different Antigone from Oedipus' daughter in Aeschylus.

Itonus is the son of Amphictyon in Pausanias, but Apollodorus makes Itonus the son of Amphictyon? Not stated; Apollodorus gives Itonus as son of Amphictyon nowhere, so unsupported here, though Pausanias does say it.
Pausanias' Delphic Thyia, daughter of Castalius (or Cephisus), is a different woman from Hesiod's Thyia, daughter of Deucalion (Catalogue of Women, fr. 7).
Apollo's lover is the Delphic Thyia of Pausanias, not Deucalion's daughter.
Poseidon's lover is the Delphic Thyia of Pausanias, not Deucalion's daughter, who bore sons to Zeus.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses the Phineus is Cepheus' brother, the Ethiopian rival suitor of Andromeda, not the Thracian seer. Apollodorus makes Phineus son of Agenor or Poseidon.
Hesiod does not make Thynus and Mariandynus sons of Phineus. Thynus is an eponym of the Thynians and not Apollodorus' Phineus child.
Mariandynus is a separate eponymous Bithynian figure, not Apollodorus' Phineus child. The link is unsupported here.
A group taken for a person; the individual daughters (Maia, Electra, Taygete, Sterope) are already linked.
A group taken for a person; Atlas as father of the Hesperides is a variant tradition, not in Pausanias, and the group is not a single individual.
In Quintus Smyrnaeus, Celtus and Eubius are sons of Meges, son of Dymas, a Phrygian killed by Neoptolemus, not Meges Phyleides of Dulichium.
Same passage: Eubius is a son of the Phrygian Meges, son of Dymas and Periboea, not Meges son of Phyleus.
Endeis is the daughter of Chiron and wife of Aeacus, and is not listed among Nereus' daughters in Hesiod; the Pausanias link confuses her with another figure.
Pausanias (Hermione) has Clymenus as a Hermionian cult name or figure for Pluto; as Hades' epithet it is not a separate sibling, so this link rests on a cult title taken for a person.
Hecate's parentage is usually Perses and Asteria (Hesiod); a Demeter-Hecate parentage is a late minor variant, and Metamorphoses does not tell it.
In the Iliad (20.219-229) Boreas sired the mares' foals with Trojan Erichthonius, son of Dardanus. That is a different man from the Athenian Erichthonius, son of Hephaestus and Earth.
In the Iliad Boreas, as a stallion, sired the twelve horses on Erichthonius' mares. This is not a love affair with the man Erichthonius, and the link misreads the passage.
Tros was the son of the Trojan Erichthonius, son of Dardanus (Iliad 20.219; Apollodorus 3.12.2). The Athenian Erichthonius is a different man.

Argus Panoptes is son of Inachus or Arestor in the other tradition; an Earth-born Argus is a confusion with the earth-born tradition; editor rules Inachus parent of Argus wrong but Earth is unsupported.

Wikipedia says Agathon was a son of Priam by other women, not by Hecuba; Hecuba's children are listed separately and Agathon is not among them.

Pindar's Angelia (messenger/report) is a personified message, not a child named Fame; unsupported guess.

In Ovid's Metamorphoses the Phrygian king Midas is not a son of the Titaness Rhea. Rhea is confused with Cybele, who is a different figure.

Pausanias names a different Thrasybulus, the Elean seer of the Iamidae, son of Æneas; the Athenian general is the son of Lycus.

Polydorus is the son of Cadmus and Harmonia in some accounts (Apollodorus 3.5.4), but the Polydorus of Oedipus the King is the father of Labdacus and son of Cadmus. Those are the same family, so this link is likely correct and should stay as is.

Midas, king of Phrygia, was said to be son of Gordias and Cybele in some accounts, but Theoi's 'confirmation' here likely reflects a different Midas; Ovid's Midas is a mortal king and Cybele is not his mother in Metamorphoses. Rhea is not his mother.
Pausanias' Thersander son of Agamedidas, king of the Cleestonaeans, is a different man; he fathered Lathria and Anaxandra, not Polynices' son.
Daughter of Thersander son of Agamedidas, a different man from the Theban Thersander.

link: Thersander parent_of Coronus, son of Thersander

Sisyphus' son Thersander is the Orchomenian father of Haliartus and Coronus, not Polynices' son.
Pausanias says the twin sons of Aristodemus (Procles and Eurysthenes) married Lathria and Anaxandra, so they are the wives of the sons, not of Aristodemus.
Anaxandra married one of Aristodemus' sons (Eurysthenes or Procles), not Aristodemus himself.
This is the Phigalian Aristodemus adopted by Tritaeus, not the Heraclid Aristodemus, son of Aristomachus.
The daughter belongs to the Messenian Aristodemus of the Aepytidae, a different man from the Heraclid.
The daughter belongs to the Messenian Aristodemus, who killed her at the Messenian war, not the Heraclid.

Boreas' mother is Eos (Aurora is her Roman name), but Aurora is a Roman figure and this is a name duplicate. The tradition (Hesiod, Theoi) gives Astraeus and Eos as parents, so the link should be Eos, not Aurora.

Poseidon fathered the Samian Ancaeus (Argonautica, Apollonius), but Apollodorus' Argonaut Ancaeus is the Arcadian son of Lycurgus; the Arcadian one is the one who hunts the boar and is the father of Agapenor.
Astypalaea is the mother of the Samian Ancaeus by Poseidon, not of the Arcadian Ancaeus son of Lycurgus.
In Ovid, Astraea is the star-maiden Justice (Aratus' Astraea, daughter of Astraeus and Eos, or of Zeus and Themis), not Nemesis; the editor has ruled that Themis is not Nemesis' parent.
Astraea is the daughter of Astraeus and Eos (Aratus; Hyginus), not Themis; in Metamorphoses she is the Justice goddess who leaves earth, with no mother named.
Ocean is a parent of Nemesis only in Pausanias' tradition; Ovid's Astraea is the departing Justice, not Nemesis.
Apollodorus calls Callirrhoe the mother of Geryon by Chrysaor, and Hesiod (Theogony 288-294) has Chrysaor wed her; the lover label is too weak for a marriage.

link: Theopompus, father of Agenor parent_of Agenor

Pausanias' Crotopus is son of Agenor of Argos (son of Triopas), a different Agenor.
Iphidamas, son of Antenor in Homer; Pausanias' Agenor link belongs to a Trojan/other Agenor, not the Phoenician.
Preugenes is the Achaean son of Agenor of Patrae, a different Agenor.
Echeclus son of Agenor is the Trojan Iliad figure, a different Agenor.
Hesiod's Demodoce daughter of Agenor is a different Agenor (Calydonian/other), not the Phoenician.

Thestius, father of Leda and Althaea, is son of Ares only in a rare Wikidata line; Apollodorus makes him son of Agenor and Epicaste.
Prothous son of Thestius comes from Pausanias and probably is a different Thestius or a variant; Apollodorus 1.7.10 lists Thestius's sons as Iphiclus, Evippus, Plexippus and Eurypylus, not Prothous.
Apollodorus 3.13.1 names a different Antigone, daughter of Eurytion son of Actor, who married Peleus; she is not Oedipus' daughter.
Peleus' wife Antigone, daughter of Eurytion, is a different person from Oedipus' daughter, who never married in Apollodorus.
Metamorphoses uses Hermione as another name for Harmonia, but Hermione, daughter of Menelaus and Helen, is a different person. Cadmus's wife is Harmonia, who is already linked.
Pausanias mentions an Electra as a Theban gate namesake, not as Cadmus's sister. Cadmus's siblings are Europa, Phoenix, Cilix and Thasos.
"Oedipus's sons" is a group label, not a person; the actual sons Eteocles and Polynices are already linked individually.
Minyas' father in the Argonautica tradition is Aeolus son of Hellen (or Poseidon), not the wind-keeper Aeolus son of Hippotes; Aeneid's Æolus is the wind king.

Ovid's Halcyone is daughter of Aeolus son of Hippotes in some accounts, but the Theoi/tradition for Halcyone follows Aeolus son of Hellen (Apollodorus), a different Aeolus; the Aeneid's Æolus is the wind king and Misenus' father is a distinct Æolus.
Misenus is son of a different Æolus (a mortal Trojan), not the wind king; the Aeneid names Juno's Æolus separately.

Lathria is a daughter of Thersander son of Sisyphus (Haliartus's father, per Pausanias), not the Theban Thersander son of Polynices.
Anaxandra belongs to a different Thersander, not the Theban son of Polynices.
Pausanias makes Haliartus son of Thersander son of Sisyphus, a different man.

Ovid's Eurynome, mother of Leucothoë by Orchamus of Persia, is a Persian queen, not the Oceanid mother of the Charites.
Erytheia is the island where Geryon lived, not his daughter; in Pausanias' tradition Erytheia is a Hesperid nymph, so the link confuses a place or namesake with his child.

Apollodorus' Amalthea is the goat/nymph nurse of Zeus, not a child of Helios; Theoi's confirmation likely rests on a namesake.
Pausanias' Alcæus is the Perseid king of Tiryns, father of Amphitryon by Laonome, not the lyric poet Alcaeus of Mytilene.
Hesiod (Theogony) and Apollodorus make Typhon Echidna's mate; Wikidata lists him as her spouse, so this was a marriage rather than a mere affair.
In Hesiod Orthus is Echidna's son, born of Typhon, and appears among her offspring. Theoi gives no union between them, so the lover link is a misreading.
Other books mean Rhea, mother of Hades; in the Aeneid Cybele is the Phrygian mother goddess and is not Rhea's child-bearer here.
Saturn's wife in Hesiod and Apollodorus is Rhea; Cybele is only identified with her in the Aeneid, so this is Rhea's link.
Saturn's wife is Rhea (Ops); Cybele is often identified with Rhea, so she is the same wife under another name and not a separate spouse.
Rhea, not Cybele, is the Titan sister of Cronus in Hesiod and Apollodorus.
Cybele is a Phrygian goddess merged with Rhea; Rhea is Saturn's sister-wife, so this sibling link confuses Cybele with Rhea or is redundant.
Demeter is the daughter of Rhea and Cronus; the link belongs to Rhea.
Hestia is the daughter of Rhea; Cybele here is a different figure, the Phrygian goddess.
Uranus and Gaia are Rhea's parents; Cybele's Pausanias lineage is sky-god and earth-goddess, but this is the Rhea link.
Gaia as mother belongs to Rhea's genealogy; the link is a conflation with Rhea.

Theseus abducted the young Helen but did not marry her; she was rescued by the Dioscuri, so she was a lover at most.

Menoetius, son of Actor, was Patroclus' father; he is not a son of Aeacus. Hesiod's Menoetius is a Titan, so the link confuses namesakes.
In the Aeneid, Misenus is the son of Aeolus, a Trojan, not the ruler of the winds or the Argonautica's Aeolus, father of Minyas.

Halcyone is the daughter of Aeolus, the ruler of the winds (son of Hippotes), as told in the Metamorphoses. The Argonautica's Aeolus is the son of Hellen and father of Minyas, so the link belongs to a different Aeolus.
The quoted sentence names only 'the other sons of Temenus' and never mentions Cerynes. Apollodorus makes Cerynes a son of Temenus, but this book's sentence does not support the link.
Misenus in the Aeneid is son of Aeolus, a Trojan, not the Odyssey's ruler of the winds, Hippotes' son.
Argonautica's Minyas is linked to another Aeolus (the son of Hellen or Poseidon's line); not the keeper of the winds.

Apollodorus (1.7.3) makes Achaeus the son of Xuthus and Creusa, and Zeus is not his father. The Zeus link seems to come from a different Achaeus, or from Phthia's son Achaeus (Phthius/Achaeus, son of Poseidon or Zeus in Dionysius of Halicarnassus), who is a separate person.

Pausanias 1.14.2 names Trochilus only as the priest who fled Argos and settled in Eleusis, with no sentence calling him Triptolemus' father; Theoi lists the Trochilus parentage separately, with no ancient citation.
Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, bore Ulysses' son Polypoetes in the Thesprotis tradition; it was not a marriage, and only Penelope is his wife, so the link is read as a lover.
A group of unnamed children is not a person; the named sons (Mermerus, Pheres) are already listed separately.

Apollodorus and Pindar make Rhode his partner, but no marriage is stated, so the link is read as a lover link.
This duplicates Aeetes, who is already linked from Hesiod; it is a spelling variant, so drop the duplicate.
Amalthea is the goat or nymph nurse of Zeus, not a child of Helios; Apollodorus's Amalthea is a different figure.

Midas is not a child of Rhea. In Metamorphoses Midas is a Phrygian king who worships Cybele's circle, and Rhea/Cybele is only his patron deity, so the link is a misread.
Statius makes Parthenopaeus the son of Atalanta and Arcadian Meleager or Melanion's line (Theban tradition: Melanion/Meleager); Ares as father is a Wikidata-only guess, and the Thebaid never says so.
Amalthea is a nurse of Zeus, not a child of Helios; Apollodorus' Amalthea is a goat-nymph/nurse, a confusion with another being.
Dirce is a Theban spring-figure, daughter of the river Ismenos or Helios only in an obscure listing; Theoi gives no support, so this is a namesake confusion.

Anaxiroe is not known as Epeius' wife; Pausanias gives no such marriage for the wooden-horse builder, and the link looks like a confusion with another figure.
Hyrmina is the eponymous place in Elis, daughter of Epeius son of Endymion (Pausanias), a different Epeius from Panopeus' son the horse-builder.
Pausanias' sentence refers to Asterion the Minotaur, son of Minos, killed by Theseus; the river-god Asterion of Argos is a different being, father of Eubœa, Prosymna and Acræa.

Pausanias' Asterion the son of Minos is the Minotaur, who is the child of Pasiphae by the bull, not of Minos; the text names him as Minos' son only loosely, but Theseus killed the Minotaur, which is Asterion, so the link confuses Minos' son with the Minotaur's name. Argonautica 3 (Apollonius) makes Eros the son of Cypris/Aphrodite with no father named, and the book never names Ares as his father. Theoi lists Ares only as an alternative tradition that the book does not tell.

This is Epeus of Elis, son of Endymion and king of the Epeans (Pausanias 5.1.4), not the Phocian builder of the wooden horse, who is the son of Panopeus.

Hesiod's fragment gives Macedon no son Pierus; the link rests only on a Wikidata claim, and the Pierus who fathered the Muses' namesakes is a different figure.

Hesiod's Theogony makes Theia a Titaness who is Hyperion's wife and Oceanus's sister. Her marriage to Oceanus is unsupported.
The Chorus is a group in Aeschylus, not an individual child. Oceanids are already linked individually.
Fall of Troy's Xanthus is the Trojan river, but the Theoi/Hesiod river-son list gives other names. This link is unsupported. The editor ruled Xanthus right only in hesiod for Midas.
Pausanias' Asterion is a different figure (Asterius), not Minos's child. In Apollodorus, Asterius is Minos's stepfather, so the link confuses two beings.

The Arcadian Pallas, son of Lycaon and eponym of Pallantion, is a different person from the Titan Pallas, son of Crius and Eurybia and husband of Styx.

Doris is an Oceanid, daughter of Oceanus and Tethys (Hesiod), and Nereus' wife; Apollodorus gives her as his spouse, not his daughter.

In Pausanias and tradition Aglaurus is Cecrops' daughter, not his wife; the spouse link from Apollodorus confuses her with Cecrops' wife Agraulos, daughter of Actaeus.
Pausanias says Cecrops married the daughter of Actaeus; Apollodorus names her Agraulos. Aglauros, Cecrops' daughter, is a different person, so the spouse link confuses mother and daughter.

Euryale, mother of Orion by Poseidon, is called Minos's daughter in some sources (Hesiod/Apollodorus), but this link is flagged as variable parentage and is not stated in the Odyssey; the tree's note shows it is unsupported for this book.

This sentence concerns the sons of Pausanias (king, exiled), Agesipolis and a young Cleombrotus, a different man from the regent.

Dirce is a Theban spring-nymph or queen, daughter of Ismenus or Asopus; no source makes her Helios' child.

This is a duplicate of the Cyrene link under another spelling.

Duplicate of Cyrene, same person under a Pindar spelling; keep one entry only.
Pausanias' Lycomedes is not Apollo's son; unsupported by Theoi.
Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus, wife of Castor; not Apollo's child.

Iliad only makes both children of Zeus in a loose sense; tradition treats Ares as Aphrodite's lover, and Pausanias gives no sibling link.
Duplicate entry of the same Aphrodite-Harmonia link, which should be listed only once.

Libya, daughter of Epaphus, bore Belus and Agenor to Poseidon in the usual tradition (Apollodorus 2.1.4), so the parent link to Agenor is right; keeping it.
Pan is not Calisto's son in Ovid; the editor limits Dryops' daughter as Pan's mother to Hesiod, and Callisto's only child here is Arcas.
Iliad 11.221-226: Iphidamas is son of Antenor and Theano's sister? No: Cisses raised him as his mother's father, so his mother is Theano's sister, not Theano.

Pindar's Hermes fathers Angelos (Herald/Message) personified; 'Fame' is a misreading, not a known child of Hermes.
Hesiod's Hymn and tradition give a nymph union with Hermes (Pan's mother); not a marriage, so lover.
Pindar's Hippolyte is Hippolyta, daughter of Cretheus and wife of Acastus, who is not the Amazon queen in Apollodorus.
Cretheus' daughter Hippolyta (Pindar) is a different woman; Apollodorus' Amazon is a daughter of Ares and not of Cretheus.
Themis is Zeus's second wife in Hesiod (Theogony 901) and Wikidata; Apollodorus 1.3.1 says Zeus married Themis, who bore the Hours and Fates.
Apollodorus' Antigone who married Peleus is the daughter of Eurytion (or of Actor), not Oedipus' daughter; the Thebaid's Antigone is Oedipus' child and unmarried.
Pandora was made by Hephaestus, not Zeus's lover.
Hermus is a river, with no clear parentage by Zeus in this book.
Eetion is Iasion's alternate name; the link duplicates or confuses it.
Pindar's Truth as daughter of Zeus is a personification; keep only if desired, but not a person in this book.

Macar is usually a son of Helios or Aeolus; the link is unsupported.
Personification; Ion makes Opportunity the youngest child of Zeus.
Leocritus son of Polydamas, killed by Odysseus, is a different Polydamas (a Trojan named in the Delphi painting by Polygnotus), not the son of Panthous.

Pausanias (1.43.5) names Astycratea and Manto as daughters of Polyidus of Megara, not the Corinthian seer, son of Coeranus, in Apollodorus.

Tantalus is son of Zeus (or Tmolus the Lydian king in some accounts per Apollodorus/Pausanias variants), but in Metamorphoses Tmolus is the mountain god judging Pan and Apollo; no sentence makes him Tantalus's father.
Omphale's husband is Tmolus the Lydian king (Apollodorus); Ovid's Tmolus is the mountain god who judges the contest, a different being.

Iphidamas son of Antenor in the Iliad; the Trojan Agenor (son of Antenor) is a different man from the Phoenician king.

Sinon as son of Sisyphus is only a late tradition (Virgil's Greek spy, said to be Sisyphus's son in post-Homeric sources); Hesiod does not say it, and it comes from an unsupported Wikidata import.
Pausanias' Crius, king of Euboea, is a different man from the Titan; his insolent son is not the Titan's child.
Pausanias' Laodice of Tegea, Agapenor's daughter who founded the Paphos-related temple, is a different woman from Priam's daughter Laodice.

Bellona is a separate Roman war goddess with no ancient source naming Juno as her mother; the Wikidata link is unsupported.

Cadmus's wife Harmonia (Hermione in some Latin texts such as Ovid's Metamorphoses) is a different being from Menelaus' daughter.
Cadmus's wife is Harmonia; in Ovid's Metamorphoses "Hermione" is the same Harmonia under a variant name (or a confusion with Menelaus' daughter Hermione), not a second wife.
Machaon is Asclepius's son (Iliad); confused with Podaleirius, who is also Asclepius's son.
Podaleirius is Asclepius's son, not Poseidon's.
Agenor of Tyre and Phoenicia is Poseidon's son by Libya in Apollodorus; Oedipus the King has no such link, so the other Agenors are namesakes.
The Doliones are a people, a group taken for a person; Dolion was their eponym.

Polybotes is a Giant, born of Earth (Gaia) from Uranus' blood or of Gaia alone, not Uranus' son in the usual tradition; Apollodorus makes Giants children of Earth.

Hopladamus is a Giant son of Earth, not of Uranus.
Pausanias' Agraulus is the same as Aglauros, already listed as daughter; this duplicate comes from a name variant.
Orion's mother Euryale is the daughter of Minos (Hesiod, Catalogue); the Gorgon Euryale, daughter of Phorcys and Ceto, is a different being, so the link confuses two namesakes.

Perses, brother of Aeetes, is the son of Helios and Perse in Apollodorus, but Perses in Metamorphoses is a different person; keep only the Colchian relation.

Aigina's mother is Metope in some accounts (Asopus' daughters), but in Pindar's Olympian 6 Metope bears Thebe; Aigina is not named as her child in this book, though Theoi lists Aegina as Asopus' daughter by Metope, so this link is a tradition-supported one.

Niobe is the daughter of Tantalus, and some sources name Dione as her mother only as a Pleiad or Atlantid namesake; the Titaness Dione is not her mother in Hesiod.

This is a group (Alcithoë, Leucippe, Arsinoë) treated as a single person. The individual daughters are the real links.

Hyperion is not a child of Agamemnon in the Iliad or Theoi's listing; Pausanias mentions a different Hyperion, apparently a misread or namesake. Agamemnon's children are Iphigenia, Electra, Orestes, Chrysothemis, Laodike, Iphianassa.
Anaxibia is Agamemnon's sister (or Nestor's daughter, wife of Pelias or Strophius); Pausanias does not make her his daughter.
